maintopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON SECURITY OF MAIL AND TELEPHONES OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday the hon. member for Yukon asked whether the government is "aware of any practice or policy in government departments whereby personal and private mail directed to members of parliament from government employees, using the internal mailing facilities of the department, is intercepted and examined by departmental or any other security personnel." The hon. member asked whether in the case of unsigned correspondence there is any procedure "subjecting the envelopes and contents to fingerprint and other identification tests."
I want to tell hon. members categorically that there is no such government policy. Inquiries have been made of the RCMP on my behalf and I have been given positive assurance that nothing of the kind is done by the RCMP or on its behalf either in security work or in connection with criminal investigation. I am not aware of any such practice in any government department or agency and certainly there is no policy or direction in that regard. I should be astonished to learn that anything of the kind is going on anywhere. Frankly, I do not believe it is. If the hon. member has any evidence that it is in fact occurring, I think he has a clear responsibility, especially since he has raised this matter and given rise to widespread specula-

If he can provide such evidence, I can assure him and this House that an immediate and thorough investigation will be made.
The hon. member for Mackenzie also raised a question on Friday with regard to the telephones of Members of Parliament. It is my understanding, Mr. Speaker, that the telephone services of members of parliament come within your own jurisdiction. So far as the government is concerned may I say, as categorically as in the case of the question relating to private mail, that there is no policy or practice by the government or by the RCMP to interfere in any way whatsoever with the telephones of members of parliament. If any hon. member has any evidence that such a thing is occurring, I would again think it is his responsibility to provide such evidence-in this case, I assume, to you, Mr. Speaker. The government would be glad to make any investigation that such evidence would suggest to be necessary or desirable.
Finally, the hon. member for the Yukon asked about long distance calls of members of parliament to and from constituents. The flat denials I have just made as to policy or practice by the government or by the RCMP in relation to members' telephones apply equally to long distance calls. There is no recording of any kind of which I am aware and certainly there is no policy of the kind the hon. member has suggested.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
That this House, alarmed at this government's inability to deal with the accumulating problems of urbanization in Canada, declares that a federal government must co-operate in good faith with provincial and municipal governments in planning and in implementing policies on revenue sharing, inter-urban transportation, housing, urban poverty, pollution and rural depopulation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in presenting this resolution and in speaking to it I wish to emphasize particularly the problems of our urban communities, although I recognize that all municipal governments in Canada are having difficulty, whether they are urban municipalities or otherwise. But the brutal fact is that by 1980 it is believed that four out of five Canadians will be living in our large cities, and so far preparations have not been made for this nor are they being made today in an effective way to meet the - problems arising within the next decade.
While these problems will deepen during the next ten years, they are already with us because in terms of transportation, housing, problems of pollution, recreation, and a decent physical environment, Canadian citizens are already facing an enormous challenge. Without any ability to control their own growth, the cities must nevertheless provide for the vast numbers of new arrivals from all over the country, and indeed from all over the world. They must deal with these vast numbers with their very limited powers, and having to rely in the main on financing largely from property tax as well as whatever help they can receive from the provinces, which is difficult in a number of cases. It may be said that under the constitution these are primarily provincial problems and that if the cities need help with their finances, that is a provincial problem. But both provincial and municipal governments are very hard pressed financially, particularly in view of the nature of their responsibilities and the growing cost of providing the services needed by the people of Canada.
In 1968, the then premier of the province of Ontario, the Hon. Mr. Robarts, summed this up rather neatly in the following statement:
The facts of life are that the federal government has the main access to the growth fields of taxation, such as personal and corporation income taxes. The provinces and the municipalities are boxed in by such slower growth taxes as retail sales taxes and in the case of municipalities, property taxes. At the same time, the provinces and the municipalities are the levels of government which are faced with the most rapidly expanding demand for services.
March 13, 1972

What the Hon. Mr. Robarts said in 1968 has become even clearer in 1972. The pressures on the provincial and municipal governments are even more severe now than they were in those days. Of course, one of the things that has added greatly to the financial pressures and the difficulties of our municipal governments-and I think this is particularly true of our larger urban governments-has been the vast growth in their welfare costs, the vast increase in the amounts they have to spend toward providing welfare for their residents as a result of the great increase in unemployment that has taken place during the last two or three years. This is directly attributable to the policies deliberately adopted by the present government. We have had massive unemployment, and as a result of this, a massive rise in welfare costs. It really does not help the municipalities any more than it helps anybody else for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to go around talking about how many vacant jobs there are in the country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
So far as our municipalities are concerned, they have been confronted by this vast increase in welfare expenditures which they have had to make as the result of federal policies, and this has added tremendously to their difficulties in discharging their other responsibilities and carrying out plans to meet the needs of citizens in these large communities. So, to begin with, the federal government should certainly share a far larger proportion of this welfare load that the municipal governments are carrying as a result of the policies of the federal government. Over and above that, because the federal government has created this problem for the municipal governments and for cities, it should be even more active, even more energetic in trying to co-operate with the provinces and municipalities in reaching solutions to these urgent problems faced by our cities.
But going beyond the present situation, going beyond the present difficulties that the municipal governments and our cities face, there are serious and urgent matters that have to be considered. There has to be some sort of national urban strategy concerned with the environment in which the great majority of Canadians work, live and play, and in which an increasing number of Canadians are going to spend their lives. In saying this, Mr. Speaker, I recognize the existence of constitutional problems. I recognize the presence of the constitutional question and the fact that it cannot be just shunted aside. But I also maintain that the constitution cannot be used as an excuse for the federal government to ignore the urban problems, as it has largely tended to do up to this time.
I am saying that the federal government must involve itself in working out a national approach to some of these problems. I want to emphasize that the provinces must always be involved in these discussions, these consultations and these policies. I am not suggesting for a moment, and I would be very much against the government of Canada in Ottawa, or even this parliament imposing plans in this area on the provinces, simply laying down here by edict, by law-if this could be done constitutionally-some program that the provinces and the cities would have to accept whether the^ wished to or not.
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems I want to emphasize that this has to be a co-operative effort in which the federal government has a role to play, but in which the provinces as well as the cities must always be involved. When I talk about the need for a national strategy with regard to growing urban problems,
I am certainly not suggesting that there should be some rigid national policies set down with which all the cities in the country have to comply. Again, even if that were constitutionally possible it would certainly be undesirable because each city in this country has its own individual profile of problems, of opportunities, and of goals. Each one has its own character resulting from the ethnic mix in that city, its industrial base, its geographic location, and all sorts of other characteristics of which we can all think. Every city has its special quality and there could be no rigid national policy that would fit the needs of all our cities, even if it were constitutionally possible to devise such a policy.
At the same time there are problems such as the tax base, such as relations between the federal government and the provinces with regard to municipal problems; there are problems involving research and co-ordination of research in relation to transportation matters. Indeed, there are many aspects of urban life that are common to all our cities. I have to say that the visible rate of progress toward effective co-operation between all three levels of government in fighting in some common way these urban problems is very disappointing.
The Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities pointed out in its brief in 1970 that there is a growing inconsistency between the low constitutional status of the city and its actual role in the lives of the people. I quote briefly:
Changes in Canadian social, economic and political organization, stimulated by the increasing demands of urbanization will soon, we believe, make new approaches to the fundamental questions of governmental organization and structure inevitable.
But we have to work with things as they are, for the time being at least. We have to work with the constitution as it now is. And regardless of what one may feel as to whether the cities are adequately recognized under our constitution, I certainly endorse the federation suggestion that municipal governments should be recognized as de facto partners in all discussions of their problems. Any attempt to ignore their existence and proceed without their participation would certainly be unrealistic. It would be virtually unthinkable.
I recognize that an approach has been made towards a process of tripartite involvement in urban affairs, involving federal, provincial and municipal governments. This has been going on for some years in such areas as housing, and I recognize that this approach has to be broadened so as to include some structure that would provide for discussion generally among the three levels of governments of urban and municipal problems. This kind of approach would seem to be the only sensible procedure to follow because all three levels of government have their contributions to make in finding solutions to urban problems.
There should not be any attempt by any higher level of government, and certainly not by the federal government, to take over. There is certainly no reason for confronta-

March 13, 1972
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems tion on this issue. After all we are dealing with the lives of millions and millions of Canadians. So, Mr. Speaker, I do not raise this subject to suggest that the government of Canada should dictate to others, should dictate to the provinces, should dictate to our cities and municipal governments. But in saying that, I do not mean to take away at all from my intense belief that the federal government must take initiatives in association with the provinces and with the municipal governments. I also believe that the federal government must broaden its interests. For example, if we think in terms of urban transportation posing a very acute problem in many of our cities, is there any particular reason, stemming from our traditions or constitutional considerations, why the federal interest in housing and in urban redevelopment should not be so interpreted as to include a consideration of and participation in the solution of transportation problems?
How can the federal government participate in a meaningful way in solving housing problems and urban redevelopment problems unless it is prepared to become involved in and help with problems of urban transportation? The federal government should be prepared to participate in studies of its own transportation policies to see how they have affected and are likely to affect the cities. This involves study of plane, train, and interprovincial bus services, as well as the federal involvement in roads. I believe the federal government should be prepared to involve itself on an urgent basis with the other two levels of government in consideration of inter and intra-urban transportation systems, and should also involve itself in commissioning and participating financially in research into these and related problems. It should be prepared to involve itself in the actual solution of these problems. How can the federal government do a meaningful job or involve itself in a meaningful way in the solution of the housing problem or the problem of urban redevelopment, unless it is prepared to get involved in the study of city transportation problems? I am again emphasizing the role of co-operation rather than the role of dictation or trying to lay down the law.
This kind of participation in meeting the problems of the city is all the more urgent, first of all, because of the extra burden that the federal government has imposed upon the municipalities as a result of the massive unemployment developed in the country and, second, because of the stand-pat position it has taken with regard to tax-sharing.
The tax-sharing agreement that will arise out of the proposed legislation before the House is really an extension of existing arrangements for tax sharing. There are changes in some details but by and large the tax-sharing arrangements proposed for the next five years are basically those that have been in effect for the past five years. In other words, the tax-sharing arrangements between the federal government and the provinces that are before the House indicate no recognition, and certainly are not based upon any recognition, of the growing needs and expenditures in the areas of provincial and municipal responsibility, especially in the large urban areas.
I remind the House again of the studies conducted some years ago by federal and provincial officials working

together. They forecast the growth in municipal and provincial expenditures in relation to the growth in the responsibility to the federal government. The federal government authorized this study but paid no attention to it. Now, we are again in the position where the government of Canada has chosen not to recognize the growing responsibilities of the provinces and cities in bringing forward a tax-sharing arrangement. Indeed, the only tangible thing the federal government has done in this area is increase the amount spent on welfare. The growing welfare burden and the general tendency of provincial and municipal responsibilities to grow more rapidly in costs, make it all the more necessary that we have active and meaningful federal participation in meeting the urban challenge in this country.
I think there was some optimism early in the year in this general area of co-operation involving municipal government and relating to municipal and urban problems. There was the Winnipeg conference in the month of April and following that a period of optimism. This optimism seemed to fade following the August meeting of the minister responsible in the federal government, the then minister of State for urban affairs, with the provincial ministers of municipal affairs and the joint municipal committee, and in the meeting in August involving the three levels of government. This was followed by a feeling of very considerable disappointment. The progress toward common policies in this area and the progress toward working together in some effective way is not noticeable. I hope the minister will be able to persuade me that I am wrong, and that much is going on in this area of which that neither I nor the country generally is aware. I must say to the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, that visible progress toward achieving common policies and some effective involvement in a co-operative way is not obvious to the naked eye.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, I am not looking for this government or any government-in fact I would be opposed to this government or any government-trying to apply an urban strategy across the board. I do not ask for that and I would be opposed to it, but we do need a national approach to urban problems which would include flexibility and adaptability. I assume that the federal government has a national responsibility in this matter. This does not mean that it can or should try to solve the problems by itself. I am convinced that the federal government can co-operate, can provide the co-ordinating framework for the cities and provinces alike. It does not have to impose itself on anyone and it should not impose itself on anyone. Events themselves are imposing the need for co-operation on all three levels of government. I do not think any of the three levels will come out of this new process of consultation exactly as it went in. I do not deny that jurisdictional disputes may arise from time to time, but that is not the point. The point is that we do not have the right to refuse to embark upon this process and should do so very quickly. We are not merely dealing with structures here, although we need an appropriate structure; we are dealing with the future of the people and we cannot allow ourselves to forget this.
It is not enough for the federal government to appoint a minister of state for urban affairs and then let matters drift, leaving the cities and municipal governments to sink
March 13, 1972

or swim in a sea of welfare costs. We need effective leadership from the federal government in this area and I say to the minister responsible that we do not seem to be getting it. I hope he can persuade us this afternoon that we are getting it, but as matters stand now progress is lamentably slow. We have no reason to believe that the federal government is meeting the challenge of the urban problems of this country.
I call upon the minister today to tell us exactly where matters stand and how he proposes to involve the federal government in a co-operative way in a significant contri bution toward solving the urban problems that are overwhelming the people who live in our cities.
In case I did not do so, Mr. Speaker, I move the motion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House deals with one of the most important and also the most difficult problems facing our people. I want to say immediately that I do not, nor I am sure does the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), blame any one person or indeed any one level of government for the immensely difficult situation in which our country finds itself. I certainly cannot undertake to go into the situation in a way that would satisfy me or anyone else in the 20 minutes available to me, but I want to make some general observations and some specific suggestions which will be followed by more specific suggestions made by my colleagues who will follow me.
The first problem that faces us is the constitution and the federal government's involvement in the urban problems facing this country. My first point, Mr. Speaker, is that urban problems are no longer local. Since 70 per cent of our people now live in urban centres, and in a few years 80 per cent or more of our people will live in such centres, urban problems are national in nature; they are no longer local and must be treated as being national in nature. Therefore, the federal role in this area is an absolutely essential factor, precisely for that reason. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, federal policies affect our urban problems in the same way as they affect all our other problems. As has already been said, economic policies which create massive unemployment add not only to the welfare rolls of the city, but add also to the problems associated with other aspects of urban life.
There are men and women who are anxious to work, despite what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has callously said from time to time. Well over 90 per cent- maybe 95 per cent or maybe 98 per cent-of those who are out of work want to work, and want work now. The Prime Minister has been guilty of a most reprehensive catering to the backlash of the hardhats of this country by trying to suggest, for reasons I cannot understand, that the problem of unemployment is not a serious one. He indicated, for example, that there were 10,000 vacant jobs in Montreal a few months ago. At least, that is what he said; yet his own manpower survey shows that in the last quarter of 1971 there were only 7,400 jobs available in the whole of Quebec. Why the Prime Minister said that I do not know.
As I said, economic policies which create massive unemployment not only add to the welfare rolls of urban gov-
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems ernments but also, unfortunately, add to our problems of delinquency, family welfare, family disruption and bring about all those other effects of idleness and humiliation that unemployment produces. That is why I am so angry about the callous way in which the Prime Minister has dealt with this problem, for he has been refusing absolutely to recognize that in addition to considering the question of unemployment insurance benefits, we must consider the human problems involving idleness and degradation which flow from unemployment. It was shameful that the Prime Minister talked the way he did about the serious problem facing our people.

speechtext:
That, Mr. Speaker, is the second reason the federal government is involved in this area. Its policies necessarily affect all aspects of urban life. Its third reason for that involvement is, obviously, that urban governments are incapable of dealing with their problems in this area, in view of the present financial structure of this country. Therefore, again, we must look to that level of government, the federal government, which has the capacity to generate funds for those activities and works which must be carried on by the municipalities as well as by the federal and provincial governments.
I repeat what has already been said. Appointing a minister without portfolio responsible for urban affairs was a useful but small step to take. And, despite the charming side of the present minister, the establishment of a new ministry will be a small step and, indeed, of no value at all unless that ministry has the imagination and determination to evolve entirely new avenues on which the federal government can play its role and retain participation in the development of useful urban policies. Therefore, the first point I make, Mr. Speaker, is that urban governments in this country, in some way-perhaps at the local level, perhaps at the level of the Canadian organization, perhaps at the level of the provincial or municipal organization, I am not particularly concerned how this is done- must be given the opportunity of direct participation in discussions and plans affecting urban life. That, as has been suggested, does not mean that the federal government must emphasize its view and impose its will on the urban level of government; rather, the federal government must have a direct part to play in this matter.
I do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that we need constitutional change for that purpose. The government hid behind the constitution for years before it summoned up enough nerve to appoint a minister responsible for urban affairs. The government has carefully indicated that that department is not an operational department but merely a coordinating department. We shall have to see if there is any difference between the meanings of these terms. I say that even under our present systen, we can set up the necessary structure and machinery to involve local governments directly in the over-all planning and budgeting for the crucial needs of our urban communities. So far, we have failed to evolve such machinery. I hope the minister will indicate any steps in that direction that may be taken.
I am not talking about an occasional conference, about an occasional meeting or about an occasional response to some demand by the Federation of Mayors and

March 13, 1972
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems Municipalities. I am talking about a permanent structure and permanent machinery, with regular consultations and regular meetings. To me, the gap between the urban needs of this country and our failure to evolve such machinery is a major gap which must be overcome if urban problems are to receive priority in our national objectives, a priority which they demand and deserve. Our urban problems, Mr. Speaker, have become so large, so overwhelming, as to be almost unmanageable, largely because of the dreadful delays in launching our concerted attack on them. I plead with the government to end these delays. Let there be no more dragging of feet on the part of the federal government, on the part of provincial or municipal levels of government, or, indeed, on the part of the citizenry of Canada as a whole.
We have talked a great deal about urban matters and about the quality of life in our cities. That subject competes with motherhood as the subject of speeches made by people at all levels of politics. Actually, though, the steps we have taken so far are miniscule in relation to the size of the problem that faces us. I appeal to the minister and to the government to start marching wilfully and in a planned way to the goal of engaging the people and municipalities of Canada in steps that will solve this problem.
The first point to be considered is the question of funds. The first problem that municipalities now have to deal with is the massive difficulties involving the problem of the availability of funds. All who live in the larger urban centres, as I do and as the minister does-I represent a Toronto constituency and the minister represents a Vancouver constituency-know about the problems that the people in urban centres experience. I am referring to the congestion, overcrowding, snarling traffic jams, deterioration of the city core, sprawling "planlessness" of the suburbs, shortage of housing, squalor of slums and rundown neighbourhoods, lack of playgrounds and parks, difficulties associated with urban transportation, dreadful pollution of the air and waters surrounding our municipalities, high cost of and greedy speculation in land, heavy cost of servicing land, and the ever increasing costs of education and welfare. These problems have evolved in the last number of decades and were not foreseen in 1867, for then the people looked at a municipal government as a little, local outfit that would have to do some minor things in society. Today, municipal governments have to deal with the major problems facing the overwhelming majority of the people of this country. Those problems require funds for their settlement. Indeed, even if we are to begin settling those problems, we will require massive funds for that purpose.
Municipal costs have risen steadily. They have risen not only absolutely but, as well, in the size of the proportion which they bear to total government expenditures and gross national product.
Let me illustrate with some figures, the latest I was able to get. In 1958, for example, municipal expenditures were 23 per cent of all government expenditures. By 1968, ten years later, they had risen to 27 per cent, an increase of between 15 and 16 per cent. In 1960, municipal expenditures were 7 per cent of the gross national product. In 1970, 10 years later, they were 9.1 per cent of the gross

national product, again an increase of some 30 per cent in the proportion of the gross national product used up by the municipalities. Therefore, there is the problem of cost that the municipalities cannot meet. What is even worse, the municipalities are forced to meet these costs largely from property taxes, the most regressive form of tax in our society.
Property tax falls heavily on the low income group, older citizens who have managed to acquire a home during a lifetime of work, young married couples who undertake to build or buy a home, as well as those who rent accommodation because invariably the landlord passes this on to the tenants through increased rents. The property tax is the worst possible and most regressive form of tax in our society. It has another disadvantage which in any discussion of the problem which the motion raises ought to be mentioned. Another disadvantage of the property tax is that it has disastrous consequences in that it distorts the objectives of our cities. Assessment becomes the major concern of municipal councils. They change plans and rezone land in their competition for industrial, commercial and other development.
In my experience, I have never known of a municipality or a planning board which started with great social objectives of building a decent city or environment which did not in the end become distorted or destroyed by the assessment demands of the property tax. The municipal council feels it has to cut corners and change plans in zoning bylaws for the purpose of getting more assessment and money. That destroys the capacity of a municipality, even if the will is there, the plan property for the quality of life for those Canadians who live in the large centres of this country.
I do not have time to develop my first point other than to just state it. There has to be a complete review of the tax base of the municipalities in Canada. This is where the federal government and the provincial governments come into the picture. We ought to give consideration to a system of unconditional grants based on some established, recognized and agreed-on formula or extend the tax base for municipalities to include some income tax or some form of other tax, or a combination of these and all other taxes. In some way, the municipalities have to be given the finances to meet their problems and carry on with their plans without constantly being frustrated and diverted by the demands for taxes and, therefore, the demands of the developers which, as I said, distorts the objectives of these municipalities.
The other point I want to make in this general introduction is that our talk about pollution will have very little meaning unless we take into account the municipal situation. Much of the pollution of Canada's waters occurs as the result of inadequate purification and recycling plants in this country. There are very few urban centres in this country that have adequate purification plants. We are talking through out hats and not being honest, in fact we are being hypocritical-and I am not pointing my finger at any one party or spokesman-when we talk about pollution and do not recognize that a major amount of the pollution of our waters as well as our air results from the failure to build the necessary purification, sanitation,
March 13, 1972

recycling and other plants in every urban community and, indeed, rural community where necessary. Until we are willing to make funds available for that, we will continue polluting the air and water in this country without taking any meaningful steps to clear up the situation. That is another area in which the federal government is directly involved.
There should be a massive program of municipal works dealing with the garbage and refuse that is created in our urban centres, large and small. That massive program cannot be carried on without major participation by the federal government. That is the kind of thing I have in mind. This kind of program would have the added advantage of setting Canada on the road to a program that would meet social needs, improve the quality of life and, at the same time, create jobs for every employable Canadian for decades to come.
I think I only have a minute or two remaining. I just want to say I am disappointed that studies in the hands of the minister have not been made public. I do not know why the minister is hiding them. I think that discussion in Canada needs the publication of these studies. Either those studies include matters which the minister is afraid to make public or there is some other reason for his failure to do so. I hope that is not the case.

Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems whereby this House blames the government for not having taken the necessary steps to ensure greater cooperation between the federal, provincial and municipal governments. This motion says among other things, and I quote:
-that a federal government must cooperate in good faith with provincial and municipal governments in planning and in implementing policies on revenue sharing-
All this phraseology is fine, and for years now we have been discussing in Canada this problem of revenue sharing, in order to enable the various governments to take care of their own responsibilities.
When I was 20 or 25 years old, I took part in the celebration of the 25th anniversary of the election of the provincial member for Lotbiniere, who was a member of the Taschereau cabinet.
At that time I did not know much about constitutional matters, but I was struck by the remarks of the late notary Verville, who was then the hon. member for Lotbiniere and who said: "How nice it is to live in Canada under the maple trees." But those were in fact pine trees and they are still there.
On that occasion I heard the rather strong speech made against the central authority by the Premier of Quebec, Mr. Taschereau. He said, the East is paying for the West. That was in 1935, when it was said that old age security pensions were paid for by the taxpayers of Quebec for the benefit of older citizens in the West.
I can also remember the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, who was at that time the member for Quebec East and later Minister of Justice in the government of Mackenzie King, who had stated exactly the opposite on the same platform. I was so struck by this that from that moment, I tried to find out who was right. From that day, I followed with great attention all political events and all federal-provincial conferences and listened carefully to all arguments put forward pro and con, depending on whether they came from members or ministers in the provincial or federal administration.
The same minister who was being made much of at the time became, two years later, a member of the federal Parliament, representing the same region, the constituency of Lotbiniere. At that time, his attitude changed.
It is my conviction that the experience acquired by these responsible men-whose sincerity I do not doubt- should allow us, in 1972, to reap the results of those years of debates of conferences at all levels and reach a conclusion establishing, once and for all, what are the real responsibilities of municipal, provincial, and federal governments, so that subsequently each level of government may avail tiself of the funds required to carry out its responsibilities.
I shall now quote from the text of the resolutions adopted in 1971 by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, as set forth in that organization's brief. That brief was presented to the Canadisn government on April 28, 1971, and I would like them to follow the suggestions made.
We talk about fighting pollution-and we have pollution indeed. Ths morning, as I was crossing the city of Montreal, they announced on the radio the degree of pollution

Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems in the Montreal area. It was .13 degree, while according to the commentator the acceptable limit is .10 degree.
There are known means of fighting air pollution. If we are to succeed, governments will have to come to an agreement on their respective responsibilities, and each will have to have the money necessary to carry out those responsibilities in order to give the Canadian people a healthy atmosphere to live in and to ensure the health of the human race.
Unfortunately, we are always faced with the same problem: lack of money. People sometimes say: Those Credi-tistes are always talking about money; they can talk about nothing else.
Last week, I attended a meeting of students who talked about their lack of money to pursue their studies. They have to fight to get scholarships. They are speaking of money when they speak about scholarships.
And here, in parliament, what do we talk about the year round? We talk of money. Whether we are discussing taxes, tax reform, the Opportunities for Youth program or the Local Initiatives Program we are talking about money. Everybody is talking about money. Why? Because money is the name of the game and also the economic blood of the nation.
We, the Creditistes, are also talking about money. We are suggesting a reform so as to see the day when this means of exchange will be truly the servant of the federal, provincial and municipal governments instead of being their master.
If we are wrong, this means that the government is right and if it is right let it prove it so that we can at last see the just society. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) is smiling but I am convinced he agrees with me. It is possible to set up a just society in Canada even though our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated, not so long ago, that no government would succeed because Canadians are mortal and imperfect.
Mr. Speaker, these same men were also mortal and imperfect in 1968 when the Liberal party introduced its program for a just society. At that time, they sincerely believed in this or they were cheating the population. If they sincerely believed in it then, they should keep on believing in it today and work for the true establishment of a just society.
In spite of our differences of opinion in this House I think all hon. members want to work with sincerity toward obtaining the highest degree of justice in this country. It is imperative for society to allow not only three Canadians out of five but each and everyone of them to enjoy security and justice in our free country. Why? Because it is possible in 1972.

WHEREAS urban development programs require increasingly larger investments-

It was reduced from 30 man-months to 15 man-months of work. Some municipalities have therefore benefited from the program, but one and a half month had been already lost since they could not have foreseen, on November 1st, that they could benefit from the program in view of the established criteria.
I remember that I had replied in this House to the statement made by the hon. Minister of Manpower and Immigration to say that I was glad of this improvement. But since it was evident, according to the minister that, and I quote:
-it is now apparent that more applications which meet the basic criteria will be received than can be approved within available funds.
-I said, as appears at page 10253 of Hansard, that I deplored certain man made actions and the fact that people who were prepared to pool their efforts in order to fulfill a need of the community could not do it. I predicted also at that time that owing to the amendments introduced to the criteria applicable to municipalities, a greater number of projects could readily be submitted. So, when I see, for instance, that $15,000 are granted to an association called the Community Hemophile Association of Toronto, to assist in the operation of its centre as a refuge for hemophiles who have adjustment problems, I do not object, but when $10,000 or $8,000 are denied to municipalities to establish a community centre from which they will benefit I protest, because in my opinion it is normal to accept programs of this nature when they are proposed in good faith by voluntary administrators in municipalities who are dedicated to the task of trying to secure some well-being in their community.
If extra money is voted, I hope that these communities will be able to start and complete their projects. I am satisfied that by this means the government will help reduce the impact of unemployment in underdeveloped areas, in the areas where the people suffer greatly from the lack of employment, from a lack in income and to enable all family heads to meet their obligations.
May I repeat this once more for the minister. Extra money simply must be given to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration in order that he may give a favourable reply to the requests that were presented, not before February 20, but before January 20. The deadline was January 31, so it cannot be said that they were received too late.
I hope that this motion and this debate will bring about concrete realizations and that at least we will be pleased to hear that the federal government and the Minister pf Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) will be able

March 13, 1972
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems to direct their officials to re-examine all these serious projects that have beep proposed so that they be accepted in order to distribute some of the wealth we have in Canada and in order to promote further in this way the establishment of the just society, something which we can do in Canada although our people are imperfect and mortal.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basford (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the three interventions so far with a great deal of interest, particularly the energetic presentation of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert). I say to him first that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) will, I am sure, note his remarks about the Local Initiatives Program. In so far as he spoke about cost-sharing with other levels of government, and in so far as the leaders of the other parties spoke on that subject, they will note that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has been in the House listening to their remarks. No doubt, he will want to deal with that issue on a future appropriate occasion.
If I may, I should like to deal with the resolution which is before us and with the remarks that have already been made. I wish to assure hon. members that for the balance of the debate today I will listen to the suggestions and comments made with a great deal of interest. I want first to express my gratitude to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) for moving this motion. I hope it does not have the same result as that which occurred the last time his party moved a motion related to a former department of mine. They once moved a motion about consumer affairs which so divided the Conservative party that they never again, during the three years I was minister, moved a similar motion related to consumer affairs. The Conservatives did not seem to be able to agree as to what their position should be in respect of consumer affairs. I hope they will be more in agreement in respect of urban policy.
As I say, I want to thank the Leader of the Opposition for his kindness today in moving the motion that he has because it is a kindness to this government when he asks us to co-operate in good faith with the provinces and municipalities on urban matters. That is preaching to the converted, if I ever heard it. The Leader of the Opposition read us a lesson which indicated that we ought to be doing precisely what we have been doing for some time, what we are doing and what we shall continue to do. It was this government that initiated, and has expressed up and down the country, the concept that urban problems and urban opportunities, so pressing, so accelerating and so far-reaching in their effect on Canada, require co-operative mechanisms and approaches from the government. It was this government that sought to persuade others to develop new mechanisms and approaches so that governments at all levels could impose shape and direction on the growth of urban Canada.
All those things that the Leader of the Opposition mentioned are precisely the reasons this government has a Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. This is what my ministry has been seeking to do, amidst some clucking of hesitancy from some Conservative elements in the coun-

try. Such co-operation is what the provincial premiers agreed to support at the first ministers conference in Ottawa last November. The motion that is before us today is, in fact, a lesson for which this government provided the Bible, as it were, in the first comprehensive study of urban conditions in Canada, a study that was published by this government entitled "Urban Canada". It was that study that provided the Bible from which the Leader of the Opposition took his text today. That study analysed the current problems and predicted the deterioration in our life, as well as the worsening and greater inequality of social conditions if trends in urban life do not change.
This government understood those prospects and formed the ministry under my predecessor. It was established, plainly recognizing and accepting two key facts; first, the Canadian fact of life, which is offered not as an excuse but as a fact of life, that municipalities are the creatures of the provinces for jurisdictional purposes, and second, that no one level of government could possibly begin to tackle urban problems in the comprehensive way that is required. These problems required the comprehensive and co-ordinated action of all three levels of government. Accordingly, my ministry's mandate states that it shall foster co-operative relations in urban affairs with the provinces and, through them, their municipalities, and with the public and with private organizations.
Our mandate is:
to co-ordinate the activities of the government of Canada in establishing co-operative relationships with the provinces and their municipalities for the enhancement of the human environment.
Co-operation and co-ordination with provinces and municipalities is precisely the purpose and the mandate of this ministry. Our mandate is broader than this, requiring us to evaluate existing and proposed policies, projects and activities, to initiate proposals for new policies and to seek, in consultation with other authorities concerned, the co-operative development of an urban policy in Canada. This ministry is instructed to initiate research and policy studies relating to urbanization and is to co-ordinate urban related research within the government of Canada.
It is a wide-ranging mandate that recognizes the crucial importance of co-ordination and co-operation within all levels of government. I quote that mandate because it was alarming to me that the Leader of the Opposition or his research staff, in what I take was a major presentation on urban policy, seemed unaware of what our mandate was and that we have within the government an instrument to do precisely what he was requesting.
I would have enjoyed hearing from the Leader of the Opposition constructive suggestions on how I could fulfil that mandate in an effective way. If he has criticisms of what is being performed, I would have liked to have heard them. But the Leader of the Opposition and his research staff seem unaware of the fact that such a mandate exists. Flowing from this mandate, there have been important initiatives and important new programs. There has been an important shift in attitudes both inside and outside the government. People are beginning to take into much greater account the urban impact on specific problems in transportation, taxation, welfare, environment, housing and so forth. The opposition motion sets out such factors as if they were separate issues to be dealt with separately.
March 13, 1972

What the motion should do is to appreciate that such problems are a part of each other and are interrelated. For instance, what one does in transportation has an immense impact on job patterns, on housing, on requirements for schools and sewers and much else that goes far beyond transportation's immediate aim of moving people and goods from place to place. I would have hoped that the Conservative motion would have recognized the essential interdependence between these various policies that must be carried out.
Similarly intertwined are those things that governments do in urban Canada, including revenue sharing, social security, immigration, creation of jobs, industrial strategy, and so on. This fact should have been reflected with perception in the motion which attempts to understand, as the opposition alleges, the accumulating problems of urbanization in Canada. We should have heard something positive from them about how such complexities can be studied, debated and acted upon by different levels of government in productive concert. That is the path upon which the government has embarked with some success, and it is to that aspect that the Opposition should be addressing itself today. The motion that is before us today affords us at least the opportunity to report just what is happening, and the Leader of the Opposition has asked for such a report. That is why, as I said, he has done me a real kindness in putting forward the motion today.
It has been the conviction of the government that we in Canada are at an urban crossroads. We know that there are serious social, economic, environmental, cultural and political questions about Canada's urban future, and some have been touched upon today. We also have, and let us grasp this important fact, more bright and more easily realizable opportunities than almost any other highly developed industrial nation. Canada's major problems of poverty, housing, transportation, environment and social equity are in fact her opportunities to create a society of special excellence in the northern part of North America. These problems and opportunities are rooted in the intensifying process of urbanization. As I have said, they are characterized by a high degree of interdependence. They are influenced by a wide range of government policies and programs at all levels of activity. If we are to accomplish our goal, there must be unprecedented co-operation and co-ordination in planning and action between all levels, or the high quality of urban life we have now will become unstuck, and that will create divisions in this country that could sunder it.
The great excitement that I find in travelling through cities in Canada is that people in those cities see other cities in North America and in Europe, many of which are huge urban areas, that have become quite unpleasant areas in which people have to live. The excitement that I find results from the realization that Canadian cities are at the threshhold and so have an opportunity not to go down that path of building huge megalopolises that are unpleasant and unrewarding places in which to live. We have a choice to take another route and to build the kind of urban centres in Canada that we want to build. That is the excitement which I see reflected in the planners, builders and politicians across the country whom I meet.
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems
I say this because I want to make a plea for co-operation at all levels. Anyone who is at all familiar with Canadian urbanization trends appreciates that intergovernmental consultation and co-operation are no longer discretionary. They are mandatory. We face a very rapid rate of urban growth. Most of our principal cities could double their populations, and our biggest cities could triple their populations, over the next three decades. These decades will require the development of more urban area than has been developed in the entire history of the country-more houses, bridges, and roads, more schools and cultural centres, more sewer and water facilities, more of almost everything that makes an urban community. This growth will be guided and shaped by policies and programs within the jurisdiction of and administered by the three levels of government. If this growth is to result in the high quality urban environment that we all desire, and that we can have, not only governments but also other public and private institutions will have to put their heads together as never before, and work co-operatively together as never before.
This government has not needed to be told that there are real problems, national in scope and transcending all political jurisdictions. That is why my predecessor, even before this ministry was formed, began talking about the need for a special study of these problems and for new tools to plan and implement public urban policy. That is why he began seeking national urban planning consultations which would, for the first time, bring the municipalities to the table. That was, and still is, a federal government initiative.
The motion before us refers to co-operation with municipal as well as provincial governments. But the trilevel consultations sought by the government have met difficulties in some provinces which objected to any major consultative role for municipalities. The Leader of the Opposition touched on some of those difficulties. Federal-provincial-municipal talks, meant to lead to some sort of structures for consultation, have been held in Ottawa, Toronto, Winnipeg and Victoria. Finally, here in Ottawa last November, the premiers of the provinces agreed to support the principle of, and I quote:
-close co-operation between federal and provincial governments toward the effective co-ordination of their relevant policies and programs.
The first ministers at that meeting instructed that:
-on-going discussions to finalize the exact elements of the consultative mechanism go forward and be expedited.
That instruction, an initiative of the federal government, broke the impasse.
The on-going discussions referred to by the first ministers had been held between my predecessor, now the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andras), and the then Ontario minister of municipal affairs, Darcy McKeough, and Mayor Marcel D'Amour of Hull representing Canadian municipalities. Changes in portfolios delayed the resumption of those discussions.
The Leader of the Opposition asked what was going on, and I am happy to report to him and announce that those difficulties have now been overcome. There is to be a

March 13, 1972
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems meeting between Mr. McKeough for Ontario, myself for Canada, and Mayor D 'Amour on April 10 at Mayor D'A-mour's chambers in Hull. That will be a meeting of the committee of which Mr. McKeough was chairman and which was instructed to convene a trilevel conference, and to work towards such a convening. We are to work toward establishing a date and a specific agenda for the first national consultation. I said, Mr. Speaker, this is to be the first national consultation, and I certainly hope it will be the first of many. I hope that meeting will show a federal initiative realized. I hope that bodes well for the future of trilevel discussion, planning and co-operation in Canada. I give the Leader of the Opposition my assurance that I will be there at that meeting, endeavouring in every way I can to ensure that it is a success and that it is productive of results for the development of further consultative machinery and mechanisms.
Our effort toward co-operation goes well beyond trilevel national consultations. The ministry has been engaged from its first day in the development of structured coordinating links with separate provinces and, through them, with specific urban regions. These efforts are now starting to show progress, despite the difficulties inherent in such a process. Links have already been established, and specific bodies created for the urban regions of Vancouver and Montreal. These have already yielded practical results of short and long-term significance. Similar links are currently being created for the urban regions of Edmonton, Calgary, Winnipeg, Toronto, Quebec City and Halifax, in all cases with full provincial knowledge, support and involvement. I know that the Leader of the Opposition would wish me well in the creation of those links.
Through such continuing tripartite structures, the ministry is placing itself in a position of knowledge and competence to stimulate and co-ordinate federal in-puts into these urban regions, not on an ad hoc problem by problem basis, as the Leader of the Opposition would have us do, but rather in full awareness of the inter-relationships of urban issues, and within coherent urban frameworks agreed to by all concerned. The ministry has focussed on key agencies in its task of establishing links within the federal government to bring co-ordination and a specifically urban view to federal policies and programs. These include, for example, involvement in major federal works in cities, in disposal of urban located military bases, in decisions regarding the management of federal lands in cities, in investigations and policies regarding urban transportation alternatives in some urban areas.
There is, Mr. Speaker, the closest consultation and involvement with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in developing new and co-ordinated approaches in housing. This involvement with CMHC extends to plans for careful intergovernmental consultation on any new approaches that materialize, after they have been presented to parliament. I want to say a little more in a minute about federal housing programs that were mentioned in the Speech from the Throne.
I wish to mention some aspects of urban transportation, a subject which is referred to in the resolution. Of course, the outstanding example is the recent announcement by

both the federal government and the government of Ontario of the site northeast of Toronto for the region's new international airport. The choice of that site was made as a deliberate stimulus to planned urbanization. As the joint announcement of the governments of Canada and Ontario stated, it was made after an exhaustive federal-provincial evaluation of potential sites. The site was chosen for many reasons that are set out in the announcement, but a major one, and one mentioned in the joint announcement was, and I quote:
-the location east of Toronto is the result of joint federal-provincial effort to provide a major stimulus to development east of metropolitan Toronto as called for in the Toronto-Centred Region Plan.
The government of Ontario has been redesigning the shape and location of some of the proposed communities in order to take the airport location into account. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the airport can provide the stimulus and foundation for an entirely new community. The government of Ontario proposes to establish such a community, which is to be called Cedarwood. The development of this new town, as well as of many of the other principal features of the Toronto-Centred Region Plan, will require the concerted application of both provincial and federal policies and programs. This must be, to a very large extent, a co-operative venture. Both governments recognize this, Mr. Speaker. The Leader of the Opposition asked what co-operation is there, and I am citing this as a specific example of specific programs that have been co-ordinated.
In its second report on the Toronto-Centred Region Plan, the government of Ontario stated:
We look forward to working very closely with the (newly established) Ministry (of State for Urban Affairs) in the formulation and implementation of many of our development policies.
May I assure you, Mr. Speaker, and the Leader of the Opposition that we are also looking forward to working very closely with Ontario in this area, and discussions to this end are now under way.
Another important part of the mandate of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs is to conduct, support and co-ordinate urban research. We are well launched into that. We have begun to study the effects of a range of current government policies on cities and on urban regions. The ministry is now designing public program impact models, of both national and big city scale, that are heavily based on computer simulation. Groups are working on the social consequences of what exists now and what we could have in such areas as housing policy, transportation, government operations affecting urban land and development, new devices to affect the use and allocation of land, and others.
Another important role of the ministry is evaluating existing and future federal policies as they affect urban areas. Our priorities for policy studies include population distribution, urban concentration and growth, government finance and revenue sharing, transportation and communications, federal land management, the character of employment to be created in this decade to meet the massive growth in labour force that is occurring, the federal role in the problems of urban poverty, and others.
March 13, 1972

You may notice, Mr. Speaker, that our various studies and various initiatives in this area cover the separate items in the opposition motion. In our research effort and in our role of evaluating existing and future federal policies, I want to assure the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) that we are not using research as an excuse for not doing anything but are acting already on the basis of information. In this kind of research and study, we are not seeking theoretical answers but practical solutions and implementation programs.
Having dealt with the ministry, may I now deal with the question raised by the Leader of the New Democratic Party, pollution. I should like to point out that the Department of the Environment has already brought in much legislation in this regard and through the agency which reports to me, Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the federal government has, with other governments, been deeply involved in pollution control by means of sewer treatment projects. The National Housing Act provides for federal loans to provinces and municipalities of two-thirds of the cost of sewage treatment facilities including a grant of one-sixth of the cost of each works. The municipalities are hard-pressed for finances, and we are all concerned about pollution. This year, we have made available more than $100 million to the municipalities for this purpose, with the provinces setting the priorities as to where the need is greatest. We have been spending increasingly more in recent years in this program, for a total to date of $500 million. The governments of Canada and Ontario have also entered into an agreement about cleaning up the lower Great Lakes, and the federal funds of $167 million will be provided through this sewer treatment program over the five-year period.
Mr. Speaker, last year and the year before we mounted colossal housing programs, programs amounting to $1.7 billion. It would be infantile to think that we could have done this without the close co-operation of other governments and the private sector. I wish to take this opportunity to thank the provinces and municipalities for this co-operation in serving Canadians. It is this kind of cooperation in good faith, pragmatic co-operation to get things done, that the urban affairs ministry, CMHC and the federal government will pursue and nurture. We believe we will continue to get this kind of co-operation from the provinces and municipalities, in many endeavours, in turn.
If I may give some statistics on the housing program that has been launched, I should like to put on the record the tangible result of the co-operation with the provinces and municipalities which I have already mentioned. In the year just passed, there were 233,000 housing units started and more than 200,000 completed. At the average occupancy rate, this is new housing in one year for more than three-quarters of a million Canadians. It is unthinkable that this could have occurred without the best co-operation between the federal government, the provinces, municipalities and the private sector. With that kind of record I will not accept a charge by the opposition that we have failed to co-operate with other important levels of government.
In 1971, the record year for housing in Canada, the federal government made available to the provinces $306
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems million for public housing. It is in this particular field that the provinces and municipalities play the greatest role. We provided $306 million for this co-operative effort for Canadians of low income in one year. In the years 1957 through 1963, the Tory government provided an average of $7.5 million a year for public housing, compared with $306 million by the Liberal party.
In 1964, the government of Mr. Pearson amended the National Housing Act to provide the provinces with an option of taking a loan from the federal government for public housing rather than the former system where the federal government had retained a 75 per cent interest. It was this amendment that paved the way for the great upsurge in the building of public housing, and which spurred the creation by the provinces of provincial housing corporations. It has been from the growth of these provincial housing organizations that the great thrust in housing in Canada has become a reality. That thrust, with the federal government the driving force, is assuring that the homebuilding record of 1971 is almost certain of being well surpassed in 1972.
With the provinces, we are co-operating in supporting non-profit organizations in housing the elderly and the handicapped. For two years with a newer thrust, that of home ownership for people of low and modest incomes, provinces have introduced complementary programs to help these home owners, with help ranging from capital grants to interest rebates. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think the mechanism of co-operation has existed in terms of building housing for Canadians. In the ministry we are developing a new mechanism of co-operation and co-ordination, not only on federal government policy but on federal, provincial and municipal policy.
I am grateful to the House, Mr. Speaker, because I think I have gone over my time. I have outlined the kind of programs and the co-operation and co-ordination which were developed and which I have no hesitation in saying will develop. In conclusion, may I say a few words about where that will lead us in terms of federal housing policy.
In the Speech from the Throne which began this session the government said that we will be proposing fresh concepts, continuing research and imagination in neighbourhood improvement, with emphasis on the need for low cost housing. We will be proposing, on the one hand, new financial mechanisms to improve the flow of funds for housing from the capital market. On the other hand, we will be proposing amendments to the National Housing Act to provide a broader range of projects for meeting the needs of low income persons and families and the improvement of urban neighbourhoods.
As a result of the steps that have been taken since 1964, such as the freeing of the National Housing Act, interest rates have increased the flow of funds from the capital market into housing to the extent that we expect the private lending institutions to finance 195,000 housing units in 1972. This funding by private lending institutions is in addition to what the government will do. This, together with the federal government's investment on behalf of low income families, will ensure that at least 240,000 housing units will be started in 1972. We believe that more can be done, particularly to improve the liquidity of mortgages held by such investors as Canada's pension funds,
