Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) for allowing me to finish my submission. I was saying that, through this legislation, a new residential mortgage bank will be proposed to parliament. Through that instrument, opportunities will be created for smaller investors to provide funds through new mortgage investment companies which will create a new source of funds for residential investment and will also provide the opportunity for small investors to invest their funds at, or near, current mortgage rates.
The amendments to the National Housing Act that parliament will be asked to consider are intended to provide a wide range of assistance to improve the quality of urban neighbourhoods. We intend to provide a wide range of choices for meeting the needs of low income families and disadvantaged groups, wherever they are to be found in Canada. We will continue to offer the strongest support to the provinces for meeting their special needs, and the federal government will also exercise its own initiatives on behalf of low income people. In this co-operative way, we will meet the housing and many other urban needs of Canadians, working in concert with various jurisdictions to maintain and create an urban Canadian excellence.
I thank the Leader of the Opposition for moving his motion and giving me the opportunity to make a statement. I listened to his presentation with interest. I can assure hon. members that I and my officials will listen with great interest to any comments and suggestions that are made in the balance of the debate.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister expressed a desire to create in Canada an urban society of special excellence. I am sure that is what we all wish. May I point out to the minister, and to the House, that there is no situation of special excellence at the present time involving the core of Metropolitan Toronto.
First, let me allude to the CMHC plans for building a low dividend, 13-story $2 million apartment house complex in my riding known as Richmond Square. Thirteen floors were supposed to have been finished by last April.

Yet, there the structure is standing, stark and empty, a ghastly sight against the sky. The building has settled in part. The people refer to the 13 floors that dip down as the "Trudeau depression", and with good reason. This is a very poor job on the part of CMHC as well as the contractor. There is no special excellence in certain parts of my riding, where about 25 per cent of the employable people do not have work. They are existing on welfare and unemployment insurance, or using up their savings when they are too proud to apply for welfare.
I confess that the situation would be far worse if it were not for the Local Initiatives Program. I must give the government some marks here, because lots of people are employed on worth-while projects financed under the LIP program. All the same, some of these projects are the goofiest projects you ever heard of in your life. I wonder what the reason is behind giving a grant of up to $12,000 to an individual or group-I am not sure which-for opening a coffee house with the emphasis on creativity. Where does all this lead us-to "spiked" coffee? I really must thank the government for approving an inordinate number of LIP projects in my riding. Out of $23 million or so allowed for Ontario, $1 million worth in projects has been approved for Spadina. This is all very well, and I appreciate it very much. I do not know whether the government is trying to elect me or defeat me in the next election. I know, however, that it seems a little strange that over $277,000 of this money, almost one third of the total approved for my riding, is to go to projects based at Rochdale College. Mr. Speaker, the government must make greater endeavours to bring about special excellence in our urban society, and especially in the core of Metropolitan Toronto.
Of all problems accumulating in the urbanization of Canada, the problem of poverty is one of the most acute. In 1967 our metropolitan areas accounted for more than one third of Canada's poor families and for more than one half of individuals living below the poverty line established by the Economic Council of Canada. A 1965 study by the Canadian Welfare Council gave equally startling and depressing accounts of the high incidence of urban poverty in Canada. The median per capita income of surveyed poor families was less than $400 in St. John's and Montreal, $500 in Toronto and $600 in Vancouver. Mr. Speaker, it takes a great deal more to live in downtown Toronto than in a village like Omemee near Peterborough. Poverty is not a problem merely of an insufficient income. It is a problem of inferior health, inadequate housing, low education and involves many other difficulties. There is no doubt that the urban poor face these difficulties to an almost intolerable degree.
The National Welfare Council's urban policy study found that 26 per cent of such families had no male head; in 43 per cent of such households there was a chronic physical problem in the family. The study also found that 70 per cent of the males and females involved had less than a grade 8 education; 46 per cent were unemployed for a period greater than ten weeks and their housing was judged to be unfit or bad, being in the lowest of possible categories in almost half of all the cases reviewed. The need for aggressive government policies to cope with this problem of urban poverty is very great. The need is immediate, Mr. Speaker, for the problem is a growing one.
March 13, 1972

The Lithwick report on urban poverty released last year warned that urban areas were increasing their relative share of Canada's poor population.
I contend that, despite the demonstrated need for a concerted federal effort to cope with poverty and, particularly, urban poverty, the Trudeau government's philosophy and policy in relation to the problem has been chaotic and inconsistent, as several examples will easily demonstrate. Last March the Lithwick report slapped the Trudeau government on the knuckles for its mistaken approach to the problem of aiding the urban poor. According to the Lithwick report, the majority of urban poor are unemployables who are not helped by manpower policies. Fully 40 per cent of all urban poor are single individuals over 65 years of age or consist of families headed by an aged person. Another 30 per cent are not in the labour force for other reasons, such as illness or handicaps. The Trudeau government has, on occasion, publicly supported the Lithwick findings. Equally frequently, it has denied the very same findings.
Consider, for example, the actions of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro). He has been known to set himself up as the champion of the cause of the urban poor against what he has called the extreme, intolerant rightism or welfare backlash. In a speech on October 10, 1971 he is reported to have said that most of the people receiving welfare in our society are not the unemployed employables. Scarcely six weeks later, he spoke about poverty and welfare to members of the House of Commons. Despite his statement that almost 90 per cent of people on welfare are totally outside the work force and often incapable of ever entering the work force, he spent the majority of his speech telling us about unemployment insurance, opportunities for youth and other job creating schemes that the federal government had authorized as part of the anti-poverty battle. Small wonder that the Toronto Star headline for the next day read "jobs, not handouts government policy for the poor: Munro". There is no doubt that the programs the Trudeau government has billed as its anti-poverty weapons are inadequate to do the job. Both manpower and non-manpower programs are at fault.
Let us consider the anti-poverty plan most publicized in recent months by the Trudeau government, the Family Income Security Plan. According to the official news release, FISP is, and I quote:
-part of a larger 'package' which the federal government has developed to fight poverty in this country.
However, the minister has forgotten to co-ordinate all parts of this so-called package with the result that there is a flaw, possibly a fatal flaw, in the anti-poverty effectiveness of FISP. The problem is that under the Canada Assistance Plan, the provinces are entitled to lower their rates of welfare assistance in proportion to the higher family allowance payments these families will be receiving when FISP becomes law. Under Section 2(b)(iii) of the Canada Assistance Plan, there is a provision that the provinces, in determining the degree of need and arrangements for social assistance to applicants for welfare, shall take into account all income maintenance payments
Federal Co-overation in Urban Problems through unemployment insurance, old age security, Canada Pension Plan, and guaranteed income supplement schemes. However, it is optional for the provinces to take into account family allowance and other schemes. Currently, none of the provinces calculate family allowance payments as income for purposes of social assistance.
However, it is entirely possible that when the new, higher benefits to poor families are paid after FISP becomes law, some of the provinces will start to include FISP as part of the welfare applicants' incomes and will lower family social assistance payments correspondingly. It is especially likely that the poorer provinces, which have long felt hard-pressed by the inflexible 50-50 costsharing arrangements with the federal government under the Canada Assistance Plan, will unfortunately feel compelled to make such a revision. This problem in the relationship between FISP and the Canada Assistance Plan is an important one, and it is essential that the Minister of National Health and Welfare take immediate steps to correct it if he is sincere in his desire to fight poverty.
The Family Income Security Plan has been a political football for the entire life of the Trudeau government. Its repeated delaying of the plan, its high-handed approach to negotiations with Quebec and its refusal to let the people of Canada in on its intentions for the plan certainly throw into question the stated desire of this government to aid those in poverty. Today, we have again heard rumours of a major change in FISP. It is to be hoped that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare change their tactics this time, that they carefully and immediately explain the changes and ramifications of these changes to the Canadian people and that they then act upon these changes in the form of legislation brought before this House without further delay.
Family allowances are not the only means stated by the federal government to cope with poverty in this country, especially in urban areas where the majority of the poor live. Manpower policies are another route by which the federal government has proposed to help some of the poor. It is not necessary to carry out much investigation before coming to the conclusion that Canada's manpower policies do not serve best those who need them most. Too much of the emphasis in manpower policies is on helping those Canadians who are able to achieve the same goals under their own steam, and too little manpower money is allocated toward helping the hard-core unemployed, the poor, and persons otherwise disadvantaged.
For example, Canada's manpower training programs have come under heavy fire from critics who point out that present programs tend to favour those persons who offer the best potential for employment to the detriment of the riskier subliterate individual who may be one of the hard-core unemployed and the poor. In many ways, the principles, regulations and practices of the manpower training program operate in such a way that the majority of resources are channelled toward those who would likely be successful on their own and away from those who really need the help.
Like the training program, the scheme of mobility grants has been proven guilty of favouring the best pros-

March 13, 1972
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems pects for success and of leaving the poor and hard-core unemployed where they seem always to have been, at the bottom of the Trudeau government's list for receiving federal aid. One survey of workers receiving mobility grants found that 75 per cent of the movers openly stated they would have moved even if the government had not offered them mobility grants. Therefore, only 25 per cent of the people were really influenced by the grants.
The catalogue continues in similar fashion. Opportunities for Youth, Local Initiatives, all are schemes oriented to the young, middle-class generation that have the information and education necessary to dream up a project and present it to the federal government, using terminology and phraseology that civil servants understand and the regulations demand. The poor and the hard-core unemployed lack this essential background. Consequently, the manpower policies and programs of the Trudeau government are a failure in helping the 13 per cent of the poor who are in the labour force, and that is the estimate of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, as well as the other poor people who could join the labour force if there were an appropriate strategy geared to meeting their needs. Indeed, an appropriate manpower strategy has many times been suggested by reputable persons.
As the Economic Council of Canada has pointed out, the federal government's strategy in the field of manpower policy is primarily a growth strategy, with the objectives of equity and stabilization clearly being secondary. I refer hon. members to the Eighth Annual Review of the Economic Council of Canada, page 98. Recently several prominent economists have been suggesting a shift in our priorities in manpower policy goals so that equity is more directly sought. The Trudeau government is urged to heed this advice. What about the other urban poor, the ones who are not helped by either family allowances or by manpower policies? According to the Lithwick report, a large number of these are the aged and female family heads with children. What is the Trudeau government doing for these people?
The Liberals' efforts to help the aged are now generally recognized as miserly and hypocritical. After boosting old age pensions by 42 cents and removing the 2 per cent cost-of-living escalator, they rationalized this move by loudly proclaiming how generous they were being in raising the guaranteed income supplement. Yet people receiving even the maximum supplement, in cases of extreme poverty, still are not brought up even to the poverty line. A single person in 1971 received OAS and GIS payments at a rate of $1,620 per year while the poverty line for them in that year was $2,013. Likewise, a couple receiving maximum OAS and GIS benefits at a rate of $3,060 in 1971 still got less than the 1971 poverty line of $3,355. Consequently, the Old Age Security and guaranteed income supplement legislation fall far short of helping the aged poor.
The hypocrisy of the government is again shown by its attitude toward females'who are heads of families. Where is the massive day-care centre plan needed to help poverty-stricken mothers who wish to get off the welfare treadmill and back into the labour market, but cannot afford to do so because of the cost of boarding children during the day? The new tax deductions for day care may help the

middle income working wife, but they are insufficient in themselves to help the poverty-stricken mother who must raise her family alone. These women also need other supportive services from the federal government.
Throughout its term of office, the government has consistently turned a deaf ear to the valid criticisms of many Canadians with regard to its anti-poverty programs. Many of these faults could be corrected without too much fuss, yet the Prime Minister and his cabinet are so stiff-necked with pride that they refuse to accept most criticism directed at them. Instead, they righteously parade their list of so-called accomplishments, and sulk with hurt pride whenever they are chided for errors and inadequacies in these accomplishments. Many issues facing the nation today are too urgent to permit such time-wasting. Urban poverty is such an issue.
The problem of urban poverty is a growing one. Present welfare and manpower programs are inadequate to deal with the problems. New initiatives, a new approach and a new commitment to solve the problem are needed. Mr. Speaker, if this government is not willing to provide these, the Progressive Conservative party is.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Official Opposition for moving the motion which is before us; it gives us an opportunity to take part in a general debate on a whole range of questions. The difficulty about the resolution and about the
March 13, 1972

debate so far is that both are so far-ranging. The matters mentioned in the resolution include revenue-sharing, interurban transportation, housing, urban poverty, pollution and rural depopulation. In such a form it amounts to a kind of motherhood resolution asking the federal government to co-operate with the provinces and municipalities in examining a wide range of urban problems. None of us in this House would deny the need to look at these matters. The minister, replying to the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), drew attention to the record of the government in showing initiative in these fields and in bringing about co-operation on a broad front in the course of these activities.
Today I shall not attempt to deal with the generality of these questions, some of which are extremely serious and will be with us for some time. Instead, I shall attempt to place one specific matter before the House and call attention to the need for further initiative with regard to it. I believe the federal government, in co-operation with the provinces, should institute a program of grants for capital and operating costs in connection with a system of underground rapid rail transit in all our metropolitan cities. If we were to pick one single priority which would contribute most in terms of an improvement to the quality of life in our cities, I think it should be this one. As a starting point, I would take every metropolitan area with a population of 500,000 or more.
The story is the same in case after case. The automobile, which made the suburbs possible, is slowly strangling urban life. I am proud to see present in the chamber some of my colleagues who have co-operated when other motions have been before the House on other occasions. I go back to the question of public transport. The automobile creates a most difficult situation for those who are responsible for municipal affairs. It distorts budget priorities. As a member of the Ottawa City Council I never heard a single taxpayer complain about the million dollars a mile it cost to build a thruway, the Queensway, for example, or about proposals for a never-ending series of rapid, limited access expressways to bring yet more automobiles into the centre of the town and put them on streets inadequate to cope with them. But many taxpayers complained loudly about suggestions that a modest subsidy be granted to the operation of a public transport system. The automobile not only distorts the budget but it benefits from an untold number of subsidies, subsidies to build those expressways, off-street parking, traffic signals, a whole range of facilities. Public transportation does not receive the same kind of subsidy or encouragement.
Apart from this, there is the whole question of pollution to be considered. Anyone trying to take a walk, even in Ottawa which I consider to be a relatively unpolluted city, finds himself plagued by exhaust fumes, the waste products of lead fuels used in internal combustion motors. They are inescapable. We learn from recent studies that more than 50 per cent of the nitrous pollutants in the air of our cities come from private automobiles. There are conditions in which fumes from private automobiles and other industrial sources of pollution can be deadly. In certain conditions, sulphuric acid droplets are created in the air, droplets corrosive enough to erode the stone of these very buildings.
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems
In the course of the great efforts which have been made to improve the national capital, some tentative steps have been taken toward improving public transportation. I had the honour to sponsor a resolution calling upon the government to enter into negotiations with the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec with a view to establishing a national capital region public transportation authority. This resolution was cast not in terms of solving the problems of a relatively small area, however important. It was designed to permit the federal government to set up, as a demonstration, the sort of arrangement which could be carried out in all our large cities. This motion was debated on March 6, 1970 as reported in Hansard at pages 4494 to 4504 and again on May 17, 1971, as recorded on pages 5872-5875. On the latter date I enjoyed the rare honour of seeing a private member's resolution passed in this House. I am still waiting to learn what consequences follow from such a signal honour. Nevertheless, it was a source of some satisfaction to me.
Today, I welcome the presence in the House of my colleague, the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) who supported me in the earlier debate. He has favoured the idea of a monorail. I have an open mind on that matter. Possibly monorail transit is the solution. But this leads us to the second aspect of the question, which is that the federal government should take the lead in an area in which the municipalities themselves are powerless to do so. It must lead not only with grants and programs but with some basic research as well.
The technology of moving men and women in vehicles other than the private automobile in peak hours from the centre of cities has to be examined through a series of research grants. Some years ago when I was a member of the Ottawa Transportation Commission I had an opportunity of going to a United States transit association convention in San Francisco, and there we looked at the Bay Area Rapid Transit system. They were building something like 75 miles of rapid transit in one fell swoop, giving rapid transit to a city that had almost forgotten what public transportation was. Before embarking upon that system they had had to establish test laboratories to find out what kind of motors should be used. They were testing two kinds of alternating current motors and two kinds of direct current motors. They had to design coaches and do some fundamental research before making the decisions appropriate to their conditions.
The reservations that I have about a monorail system are twofold. First, there is a major switching problem of going from one line to another. The system seems to be adaptable for use as an airport line; for example, going from the centre of a large metropolitan area to the airport serving the community and back again.
Then, there is a major question concerning weather conditions. We are faced with ice and sleet, which is a severe test in wintertime, and these conditions do create problems for public transportation systems. I note that the famous Turbo train which operates between Toronto and Montreal ran into continuing technical difficulties, and had an accident resulting from weather conditions a few days ago.
774

March 13, 1972
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems
Surely one of the very specific areas in which the government of Canada can take the initiative, consistent with our constitutional position and with the rights of provinces and municipalities, is in the area of public transportation. If a city is desirous of establishing an underground transportation system, such as Montreal did for Expo, the provision of some research grants would produce some conclusive and reliable evidence as to whether to develop a rapid transit system consisting of steel on steel or rubber on steel. Montreal made its decision based on the fact that they had to meet a serious time factor, and as a result their system was a costly one.
I am glad to see the minister is paying careful attention to my remarks, and I am delighted to see him here. I think that federal initiative in this area should be geared to the specific conditions prevailing in Canada, to the kind of cities we have and the kind of population densities we have in those cities, and to the immense difficulties we have to face in trying to plan forward in cities when we do not know what the fixture holds. An underground rail rapid transit system, could be the key to the kind of densities that you would have in centretown, to the use of the most expensive real estate, to the patterns of transportation which flow from the centre of metropolitan areas through an interurban pattern. The technology has to be established, and it can be established only with financial assistance at senior levels of government.
I have touched on just one problem. I am sure members on the other side of the House are interested in this matter and will give us their views. In my submission, this is one specific area in which it will be possible to make a positive contribution to the quality of life in our cities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate on the motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), which reads as follows:
That this House, alarmed at this government's inability to deal with the accumulating problems of urbanization in Canada, declares that a federal government must co-operate in good faith with provincial and municipal governments in planning and in implementing policies on revenue sharing, interurban transportation, housing, urban poverty, pollution and rural depopulation.
I should like to put some emphasis on the question of rural depopulation. The nature and extent of rural depopulation in Canada has severely damaged the quality of life in rural Canada and has aggravated many of our urban problems as well. The Progressive Conservative party has committed itself to revitalizing rural Canada. This is an important aspect of providing more humane and manageable urban development. The following resolutions were formally accepted by our policy convention at the Progressive Conservative annual meeting on December 5, 1971.
1. Federal policy should recognize and develop the importance of Canadian towns and other communities under 10,000 population, in the following ways:
(a)	Present national policies which in fact now hurt or with change could help Canadian small communities should be systematically reviewed and changed.
(b)	Meetings should be convened with the provinces to develop a national policy for the towns and rural communities of Canada.
(c)	There should be consideration of establishing an objective "Towns Test" to determine the effect upon smaller communities

of every piece of new legislation proposed for consideration by parliament or for implementation by order-in-council, and a National Council from the towns to ensure a liaison between the national governments and representatives or local government, to meet quarterly for two-week periods in Ottawa to review legislation and practices which affect smaller communities and rural Canada, and to make recommendations informally to standing committees of parliament and government departments and prepare a formal annual report to parliament.
(d)	Public servants whose decisions seriously affect Canadian small communities should, wherever possible, have personal experience in small communities and should be required to spend an annual two-week sabbatical in a different town or rural community, in a different region each year.
(e)	In consultation with the provinces, professions, and representatives of small communities, there should be established a small agency of lawyers, economists, and others, independent of federal government in the manner of a Crown corporation, supported in part by the subscription of local governments, and available to assist member local governments, when they are engaged in major confrontations with groups whose expertise or other power is disproportionately strong.
It Is now the unique good fortune of Canada to possess both great cities and strong smaller communities. Any serious weakening of Canada's smaller communities would involve a high human cost to the people forced to move, a high dollar cost to the cities forced to receive them, and a higher cultural cost to a country which values the qualities of life in smaller communities.
There is evidence that smaller communities can be both viable and valuable to Canada. Roughly 35 per cent of Canadians interviewed in the 1966 census live in communities of population less than 10,000, and the general quality of Canadian life is enhanced by the continued existence of communities where there is a sense of place, a sense of neighborliness, a tradition of responsible participation in local affairs, and a respect for environment.
While it is recognized that the provinces are responsible for municipalities, it is also recognized that many areas of federal responsibility nevertheless seriously affect smaller communities in Canada, and that it should be a conscious policy of the federal government to co-operate with the provinces in developing the full potential of these communities. Present national policies concerning transportation and transportation services, housing, industrial development, agriculture, taxation, trade and other matters often harm or fail to benefit smaller communities in Canada. The official harm done these communities, while sometimes deliberate, is often simply the result of policy makers ignoring or not knowing the interests of smaller communities. The limited budgets, limited experience and limited expertise of smaller communities often place those communities at a serious disadvantage in dealing with governments, agencies, corporations and other powerful groups.
There is now virtually no effective federal provision to help provinces or smaller communities meet the special problems and opportunities of smaller Canadian communities. Leadership by government in recognizing the potential and value of Canadian towns and smaller communities will encourage private industry, institutions and individuals to recognize the viability of such communities. A Progressive Conservative government of Canada will encourage and strengthen smaller communities, as a
March 13, 1972

necessary complement to the continued growth of large urban communities and attitudes. A Progressive Conservative government will undertake a systematic review and amendment of all national policies which in fact now harm but which with change could help smaller communities including, specifically, policy respecting housing, industrial development and incentives, resource development, railroads and other national transportation, the Canada Council, the CBC and other national cultural institutions, agriculture, manpower, taxation and trade.
A Progressive Conservative government will convene meetings with the provinces to work out a national policy for the towns and rural communities of Canada. A Progressive Conservative government will consider, as one step, the establishment of a special small communities branch in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to, first, maintain in co-operation with the provinces and local communities an up to date inventory of industrial opportunities in Canadian smaller communities; second, to ensure the inclusion of small community representatives in certain Canadian trade missions and government-industrial briefings; third, to circulate to local officials the latest information on trading and industrial developments of importance to small communities; fourth, to prepare and circulate an annual report on technological and other changes which allow modern industry to move outside cities, and a list of the kinds of industry so liberated; and, fifth, to otherwise assist the development of a modern industrial base in Canada's smaller communities.
A Progressive Conservative government will consider the establishment of an objective test, perhaps to be called a town's test, to determine the effect upon smaller communities of every piece of new legislation proposed for consideration by parliament or for implementation by order in council.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to preface my remarks by congratulating the minister on his appointment as Minister of State for Urban Affairs. I would remind him that when he was Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs I tagged him as the national shadow-boxing champion of Canada, for the simple reason that under his ministry Canadians had the highest priced drugs than ever before. He has assumed the mantle of Minister of State for Urban Affairs when Canadians are paying the highest prices for housing we have ever experienced. I hope that when he re-reads the speech he made today he will, in all humility, appreciate that Canadians are paying the highest price for housing that we have ever experienced.
We in the New Democratic Party agree with the motion presented by the Progressive Conservative party and we share the alarm expressed because of the government's inability to deal with the problems of housing and urbani-

March 13, 1972
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems zation. Indeed, we share the alarm of most Canadians, not only in respect of the inability of the federal government to deal with these problems of urbanization but the inability of the provincial governments.
I think it would be fair to say that this federal government to the present time has shown lack of leadership, slowness of response and lack of co-ordination and planning in respect of the problems of urban life. It could be said that the provinces also have been guilty of lack of co-operation, participation and determination as well as lack of appreciation of the magnitude and urgency of urban problems. Having blamed both federal and provincial governments, I would imagine most Canadians would say, "Plague on both Houses", but I am a charitable person and would like to think that these problems are not directly the responsibility of either the federal or the provincial governments: they are an accumulation of problems as a result of urban growth in an industrial society. When one realizes that by the year 1980 two-thirds of all Canadians will be living in 29 major Canadian cities, one appreciates the impact of these problems and the necessity to tackle them. This also indicates the urgency of the need for co-operation and co-ordination.
When I heard the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) speak about the mandate of his government I was reminded of the year 1967 when the federal-provincial conference on housing and urban development met. At that time Mr. Pearson took the initiative and suggested the establishment of a national urban council to take on the problems of the big cities through a tri-level approach. I was also reminded of the rejection of this proposal by most of the provinces. It was the predecessor of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs who reintroduced the idea in 1970 and then, rather cautiously but persuasively, tried to impress upon the provincial governments the need for a tri-level approach to our major problems. In November of 1971 all the provinces made a commitment to form a national urban council. From that time to today, when the minister announced that there will be a meeting in April of this year of federal-provincial-municipal representatives, we have been left in the dark with regard to the problem.
As has been indicated by some of the provinces, there has been a change of attitude. The province of Ontario has attempted to approach the problem from the point of view of tax sharing revenue, which would probably scuttle the structure of a national urban council. Today we find that the minister has announced the meeting for April. One wonders just how long it would have taken the minister to announce the meeting if the opposition had not brought forward this motion today. One wonders what political advantage he was attempting to gain by holding off and keeping quiet.
I should like to deal very briefly with one of the major aspects of this resolution, that is, the aspect of housing. May I remind members of the House that in April of 1969 we witnessed the resignation of the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) because the government refused to implement the recommendations of the task force report on housing. From that time there has been no legislative program on housing by this government and we have had
[Mr. Gilbert.)
very little new programs in the housing field: no legislative changes have taken place since.
The predecessor of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs was a man who dedicated his time to research rather than to action. He surrounded himself by academics and consultants, and instead of tackling problems he attempted to research them. We now find that the problems are still with us, but the minister has left us. The previous minister appointed Harvey Lithwick to make a study. He came forth with a report entitled "Urban Canada-Problems and Prospects". Today, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs called it the bible. I might say that probably he and many others have not read Harvey Lithwick's report. I hope that after the minister reads it he will take some action on it, because when he calls it the bible this might mean that, like the bible which usually sits on the shelf and accumulates dust, the same might be happening to the report.
As to Harvey Lithwick, he resigned in disgust because of lack of initiative of this government with regard to implementing the ideas that were set forth in his report. He revealed the bureaucracy and empire building that goes on within the department and then took the obvious course and resigned.
The minister's predecessor appointed Walter Rudnicki to set up a new policy and planning division. He also appointed Michael Dennis to prepare a report with regard to social housing, in particular low cost housing. He also had a task force to report to him within one year on what changes should be made to the National Housing Act to meet the needs of the seventies. None of these reports has been made public, although the minister has had them in his possession for some time. I call on the minister to exercise participatory democracy by divulging to all Canadians what was contained in that report.
Canadians should know what they have paid for in obtaining consultants to prepare reports concerning the housing and urban problems in Canada. I do not think the minister should take upon himself the decision to keep these reports secret. He should make them public and refer them to the appropriate committee for study and discussion. It is only by hearsay and from articles that we know what the reports contain. In a recent article by Michael Audain, entitled "Housing and People", published by the Canadian Council on Social Development in the December 1971 issue, he attempted to point out the gist of some of the recommendations which Canadians have paid for and which the government is keeping secret. The first recommendation is as follows:
CMHC should be restructured and reoriented to change its role from that of primarily serving as a public lending institution to one capable of devising comprehensive and socially sensitive housing policies for the federal government, the implementation of which might in many cases be devolved to provincial and local agencies.
We have seen the performance of this government in the past few years, namely, that of a friendly banker being slowly pushed into developing a program to assess the comprehensive needs that Canadians have with regard to housing. We agree with this principle and we urge that the federal urban council be set up immediately because it is needed to assess, to plan and to co-ordinate housing needs across Canada and, as the minister said, not only housing
March 13, 1972

needs but the impact with regard to pollution, transportation and many related problems. We agree with that and we ask the minister to change the role of a friendly banker to one of active participation in developing a comprehensive program of our social needs in housing. The second recommendation in the report is as follows:
The federal government should undertake an aggressive land assembly program to stem the most inflationary factor in housing costs: the price of land. This program would involve a considerably greater financial commitment than the $100 million that CMHC has spent on land assembly in the last ten years and a much more direct relationship with municipalities.
Of the three cost items with regard to housing today- land, building materials and interest rates-the greatest increase in cost has been in land. It is high time that the government took the initiative with regard to a land assembly program initiated by them in co-operation with the provincial and municipal governments. I am reminded of the experience of the hon. member for Trinity when he attempted to direct moneys to municipalities for housing, and the storm that he encountered: it was probably one of the major reasons he resigned. For the edification of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs may I quote the words of a British expert, Professor John Donnison of the London School of Economics who, speaking in Canada in 1968, said:
Municipal authorities must act quickly to acquire large tracts of land, before they are actually needed, and under compulsory powers if necessary, to counteract the problems of fast-rising land prices in urban centres. Buy more land now, rather than try to control prices. The land thus acquired can be leased to private developers, for example, when the time is right for development. Such programs may call for a large initial investment by the government, but thereafter they generally cover their costs or make a profit.
The government, even though it has had the mandate, has not acted with regard to land assembly. It is time the minister set forth in his capital budget the amount of money he is prepared to make available to the provinces and municipalities with which to acquire land. If he does not, we will have a continuation of the speculation that prevails with regard to housing and we will experience ever higher costs of land.
The third recommendation of the task force is that a new section regarding housing rehabilitation should be written into the National Housing Act. Under its provisions, low-interest rate loans would be made available to landlords and homeowners prepared to improve their homes without displacing present occupants. May I remind the minister that home improvement loans in Canada have been on a steady decline for the last four or five years. It is high time that grants and low-interest loans were made available for people to rehabilitate and rebuild their homes. It is not sufficient to give such grants and loans to landlords without taking into account the necessity for rent control or strict adherence to housing maintenance bylaws: otherwise, the money goes to subsidize slum landlords who do not pass the benefit on to their tenants.
The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) has often asked for the provision of such low-cost loans and has told us of the experience of old age pensioners who
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems live in cities and who want to repair their homes but do not have the necessary money to undertake repairs. Surely it is time for the minister to make available to municipalities moneys so that it can be loaned to houseowners, who in turn will repay these loans at very low interest rates as part of their taxes. It is not the duty of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs to protect the banks and insist that people go to banks for home improvement loans. He has a duty to take care of people who cannot obtain loans from banks and cannot pay the high interest rates that are demanded. I urge the minister to take note of this suggestion.
The fourth recommendation that might be incorporated is an important one: it is that the federal government should reduce its spending on subsidized public housing to a point that might lead to eventual abandonment of the program. This is a recommendation in the report that the government has in hand. It seems that the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) is still haunting us!
In his task force report on housing development, he said, "Away with public housing!" He made it the whipping-boy. Instead of attacking the problem which shows that housing needs cannot be met through the private market, he made public housing the whipping-boy. I hope this minister does not fall into the same trap and follow that line of argument. The so-called stigmatization of the social environment by public housing is something that is completely false. I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that only 10 per cent of all 1970 starts were in public housing. I remind the minister that the Senate Committee on Poverty has urged an expanded program of public housing. Surely it is time that we built public housing which would be satisfying for people to live in, embracing some of the ideas and initiatives that have been tried in European countries? As in England, we could have municipally-owned public housing. We could develop co-operative housing as they do in Sweden and adopt the idea of rent allowances as in Germany.
I notice that my time is drawing to a close, Mr. Speaker, and therefore I wish to direct my final remarks to the interest rates that people pay for housing. The minister expanded his chest and boasted that legislation has been prepared with regard to a residential mortgage bank. Isn't it high time that he directed his efforts to our high interest rates, the highest we have ever experienced in Canada?
There are four things we need in Canada: a right to housing, a right to medicare, a right to employment and a right to education. It has been said many times that every Canadian is entitled to clean, warm shelter as a matter of basic human right. I call upon the minister to forget the banks and lending institutions and direct his attention to lowering interest rates so that all Canadians may live in decency.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Watson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the minister had assumed the functions of Minister of State for Urban Affairs. In his three years as consumer and corporate affairs minister he brought in 12 new pieces of consumer legislation-more legislation in the consumer field than we had seen at the federal level in the last 20 years. His experience in consumer affairs is the right kind of background for the public housing role which has become the pre-eminent concern of CMHC during the past several years. Just to show how important that role has become, in 1971 the government of Canada made $306 million available for public housing. The public housing impact has pushed housing unit starts to new records-to 233,000 starts last year and over 200,000 completions in 1971, while at least 240,000 starts are forecast for 1972.
There is no lack of activity, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to pose the question about the quality of this activity in terms of the kind of living conditions we will find in all these new subdivisions, condominiums, limited income and various low-cost housing five or ten years from now. I represent an area which reflects the accommodation and living problems which plague major Canadian cities. What I find most frustrating is that we seem to know pretty well the way in which most of the problems should be solved yet we continue to commit the same errors of planning, the same unco-ordinated, unaesthetic development of subdivisions and apartments that characterize most of our suburban landscape whether it is outside Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg or Vancouver.
The Speech from the Throne indicated what the minister reiterated today, that the government intends to introduce new measures to provide a wider range of assistance to improve the quality of urban neighbourhoods. This program will replace the urban renewal program which the previous minister dropped last year because it tended to encourage the bulldozer approach to urban renewal. The new program will stress urban rehabilitation, a concept of which I heartily approve.

However, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the result-certainly unexpected-of the decision by the department to drop the urban renewal program.
Two municipalities in the riding of Laprairie, namely Greenfield Park and Laprairie, had undertaken some rather expensive studies under the urban renewal program with the idea that they would receive subsidies from the federal and provincial governments. When the program was suddenly terminated last year, these municipalities, which has undertaken these studies in good faith, found themselves saddled with considerable expenditures which were unexpected and not provided for in their estimates.
I think that it is altogether unfair, on the part of the federal government, to refuse to honour the obligations that it had agreed to assume when Laprairie and Greenfield Park ordered studies under the urban renewal program.
I strongly advise the minister to make sure that the department recognizes what I consider to be its moral obligation toward Greenfield Park and Laprairie.

While it appears from the Throne Speech and from what the minister said today that much will be done to improve the quality of urban neighbourhoods, I ask: What about suburbia? When will we realize that by giving a stronger social animator role to CMHC we could, at practically no additional cost, vastly improve our expanding suburbs. This social animator role on the part of CMHC would necessarily reflect the needs of any given area.
I do not think the corporation could expect to play the same sort of role in all areas across Canada. For example, in the national capital region it is time that CMHC, in co-operation with the National Capital Commission, started pushing for underground electrical wiring and underground telephone cables. A street not far from Parliament Hill was completely ripped up last summer. I happened to travel over it at that time. A few months later I noticed that although the street was fully repaired, one side of the street was a tangled network of telephone and electrical cables. I am sure, since the city of Ottawa had spent hundreds of thousands of dollars repairing the street, that at very little additional cost it could have put these electrical and telephone cables underground. However, it is not possible, apparently, for the National Capital Commission or CMHC to force these kinds of measures on the city.
We who are in public life find that too many people take too many things for granted. For instance, to the average citizen it seems that governments think out solutions to all kinds of problems more thoroughly than is the case. Such an assumption is in error, as is evident when one comes to this place. I also think that different levels of government assume that other levels of government are thinking more about problem solving than is the case. Here we find the city of Ottawa allowing overhead wiring to exist even though opportunities present themselves for placing these wires, at low cost, underground. I feel that in an area such as this the National Capital Commission and CMHC in concert ought to exert some influence. These bodies should adopt an innovative, social-animator role in the Ottawa area and put pressure on the municipal council to act.
In other parts of Canada the role played by CMHC might differ. Along the south shore of the St. Lawrence, in the federal electoral district of Laprairie which I represent, one finds that many things have not been done that should have been done. For instance, many municipalities are still encouraging new housing subdividers to come in without properly capitalizing the costs of all services related to such subdivisions.
The municipalities look at obvious things such as sewage, water, perhaps sidewalks, and capitalize the cost of those services; that is, they apportion over a fixed period the capital costs against people who will live in the neighbourhood or subdivision and will have to pay these capital costs through taxes. However, the rest of the people in the municipality end up paying for a whole host of other costs associated with the development of any particular subdivision. I am talking about things such as interest charges, street lighting, police services, fire services and administrative services as well as the many small items that do not look very large when provided for
March 13, 1972

a single house but which add up very quickly when provided for a 200- or 300-house subdivision. These costs become a serious tax burden for the taxpayers of a municipality.
Now, in some parts of Canada, provincial governments are requiring adequate capitalization to provide such services so that they are included in the price of the lot. This, however, is still not occurring in Quebec. I suggest that in areas where provincial governments do not take on the necessary innovative or social animator role CMHC should exert indirectly the kind of pressure that is necessary to protect the average municipal taxpayer.
Let me talk about planning. Generally speaking, I feel that there is lack of local and regional planning because we are still putting low-cost housing into areas that really cannot afford to support it. Houses go into a small municipality: taxes are low when they first go in; however, by the time people start paying through taxes the various costs associated with the development of such low-cost housing, the people who first went to that municipality to take advantage of such low-cost housing find they are paying astronomically high tax bills. I feel strongly that CMHC, the organization for which the minister is responsible, should not allow low-cost housing to go into a municipality that does not have a sound tax base. In the long run we are only inflicting higher costs on the people we are supposed to be helping if we allow that type of housing to go into a municipality which does not have a sound tax structure.
There are several other areas in which CMHC can act in an innovative and animator role. We should concentrate more on architectural standards, for example. The amount of space which CMHC insist on being devoted to green areas is not large enough. In Montreal, at least, this green area rule has not been vigorously enforced. In many cases we find that designated green areas have been rezoned by towns after a period of years. There appears to be no real guarantee in law that such green areas will be kept green or as park areas for the benefit of local populations. CMHC should be very much more vigorous in enforcing this green area rule and in eliminating from its list of acceptable municipal areas any towns or municipalities that renege on their original green area agreements. This has happened in almost every municipality of the south shore that has benefited from CMHC or NHA funds.
Also, CMHC does not protect the consumer enough. They do not appear to regard themselves as the protectors of house buyers. They feel that their legal obligation is to make sure that a house bought with CMHC guaranteed funds is structurally sound and it ends at that. I feel that under the guidance of the minister, CMHC can become much more consumer conscious and more of a protector of the house buyer no matter whether that buyer buys a low-cost house or a more expensive suburban house that is backed by an NHA guaranteed loan.
More public input into CMHC decisions is needed. It would be distinctly to our advantage if there were more public input into deciding where subdivisions are to be placed, into what areas around any large city are to benefit from CMHC funding of public housing, etc.
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems
We hear a great deal about the quality of life these days. The minister has more potential for upgrading the quality of the living conditions of Canadians than any other individual in this country. I am confident that this is the kind of challenge the House relishes and I implore hon. members to take hold of CMHC with both hands and mould it into the innovator, social animator and consumer protector role which this country needs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the specific failures charged to the government in the motion we are considering is that of dealing effectively with the problems of pollution in the urban environment It has become fairly obvious that pollution goes hand in hand with urbanization. The problems we face in our cities are such interrelated parts of a vicious circle that no single thread can be found and no problem can be easily pinpointed without including in that the question of pollution control. Since 1968 the present administration has enacted some legislation relating to pollution. In a sense it can be said that the government has acknowledged its obligation to the Canadian people to deal with pollution problems in this country. However, if we look at the bills that have been passed and the effect they have had in the 31 years of this administration, we find we have made very little progress in pollution control per se and much less in terms of pollution control of the urban environment.
We have had amendments to the Canada Shipping Act regarding marine pollution. The government has created the Department of the Environment with the express intention of co-ordinating all pollution control efforts. We have had the Clean Air Act, the Canada Water Act, the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act and several others-but none of these pieces of legislation deals directly with the problem of pollution in urban areas. Not only that, none of these bills has yet become an effective part of the law of Canada. I could go through them one by one, but I will not do that at this time except to mention the Canada Water Act which was brought in with great fanfare in 1969-70. However, to my knowledge it has not resulted in any agreement in the two years it has been in existence to effectively create pollution control projects. There have been some studies but no actual accomplishment.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS
