subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
The same goes for the Clean Air Act. It has not yet been effective. The control of urban pollution has been largely left to the provinces and municipalities. This has resulted in a very unco-ordinated attack across the country on pollution control and urban centres. When it comes to the field of pollution, the federal government seems to hide behind the constitution. Thus, the activities of federal departments for airports, expressways, bridges and public buildings seem to be immune from urban planning and environmental control. So are the activities of federal enterprises responsible for harbours, railways terminals and corridors, power plants, telephone and other utilities.

March 13, 1972
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems
However, taken together, the significance of federal involvement in urban areas is very high because more and more the federal government is taking over large segments of the economic life of this country. There are more federal departments, federal buildings, harbours, airports and everything. In large part this is causing a problem rather than helping to solve it. The presence of the federal government as employer, developer and taxpayer in our larger urban regions will almost inevitably increase in the future. If urban problems at all levels of government are to be harmonized with environmental and related urban problems, it will be difficult to avoid the conclusion that relevant federal agencies must participate actively in community planning. Until this time they have managed to be exempt, in large part, from community planning and regulations that control everybody else.
I would now like to get down to specifics. Water and air pass freely within, between and over all political jurisdictions in Canada. They know no boundaries. Hence, all jurisdictions have a necessary role to play in their management. The sad part of the whole mess is that most cities do not know how much air and water pollution they actually have. If they do know, they are not telling their citizens. People who live in Toronto happen to know about air pollution measures because the Ontario government both monitors its urban air and takes corrective measures after monitoring. The federal government recently announced it was undertaking a national survey of air pollution sources and the amount it would cost for clean-up. I hope this survey produces fruitful results-but surveys are only the beginning. We have had air pollution problems for many years, but the federal government has always backed off them and has said it has no responsibility and, therefore, has taken no action.
Under constant pressure from pollution control groups, members of this House and members of the public, the government has admitted it has responsibility in connection with air pollution: it has undertaken to expand its air control facilities. It is only now, at least ten years too late, that it has expanded its control system far enough to even know the whole picture across the country. Even if cities are ill-informed on air pollution, about which there has been some argument, every city should know what it is doing to its water because of sewage. Given the increasing urbanization trends in Canada, the sewage treatment situation in our larger centres is of the greatest significance.
Quebec City and Montreal treat virtually none of their sewage, while Vancouver treats only 30 per cent. In fairness it can be said that over the years these large cities have had the sea at their door and the sea has been considered a wide-open and limitless dumping place for all kinds of waste and sewage. We are now finding that this is not true; it is not limitless and there are areas where sewage comes back on people further downstream. These responsibilities are now beginning to be recognized. The remaining large Canadian centres such as Toronto, Edmonton, Ottawa, Hamilton, Calgary and Winnipeg treat up to 100 per cent of their sewage at least in a primary way, but only Toronto and Edmonton, as far as I know, provide more than primary treatment for their sewage.
Expenditures on urban water treatment facilities have been growing at the rate of 8 per cent per year nationally.

This is faster than the national population growth. However, much higher levels of expenditure are necessary if our urban areas are to catch up with their backlog and treat waste-water discharged by their new populations and industries to minimum acceptable standards. Not only do we need an air monitoring survey, as I mentioned previously, but we must conduct a national industrial survey to determine the exact breakdown of the wastes from every plant in this country which is discharging waste. This information is not available to us. Work has only just begun in dealing with some of the major pollutants. It is true that several bills have been passed in this House, but they have not yet become effective.
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) shows great interest in his department and a real concern for the quality of the environment-but it takes more than one minister in a cabinet of 30 to provide the impetus and the funds which are required to control pollution. There must be a commitment by the government as a whole to give priority to pollution control. It is not sufficient just to set up a Department of the Environment and allow one minister to make speeches and bring down legislation: financial backing is necessary, and this has not yet been accorded.
I wish to consider for a few moments the case of the automobile. The automobile is about the worst polluter of the air. In the larger population centres, it is the worst. Conditions in Montreal dramatize the situation facing all Canadian cities, in some of which carbon-monoxide levels are higher than they are in many large United States cities. Statistics relating the total number of vehicles in Canada to the number of miles of highway are not sensible, inasmuch as motor vehicles in Canada are concentrated in relatively few areas-within half a dozen of the major urban centres. This is where the threat is developing. Little has yet been done. City planners have been telling us for years that private automobiles have no place in the centres of major cities. As long as automobiles cause pollution, cars should be kept out of the central cores of urban areas where, in any case, other pollution levels are high. Experiments are taking place in an attempt to produce vehicles which do not cause pollution. They show promise, but obviously it will be a number of years before there is any hope of our seeing these vehicles in common use.
As to getting industry to clean up its own mess, the budget of last June announced the withdrawal of sales tax on anti-pollution equipment. This is a step forward, one for which our party and others have been asking for a long time. The government has shown wisdom in taking this course. I understand there was to be a loan fund to assist industry in meeting the cost of installing new pollution control equipment. The Minister of the Environment has been talking about such a fund, but we have not seen evidence of it yet. I hope something may be done soon along these lines. It is generally accepted that if a corporation operates a plant which regularly discharges pollutants into the atmosphere, it should be punished. Before punishment is imposed however, the firm concerned should be given a chance to improve the situation and see that no offence occurs.
March 13, 1972

I wish to mention, in passing, another aspect of pollution in urban areas-the disposal of garbage. This is the ugly side of plenty. Solid waste produced in Canada is estimated to be 673 million tons a year. Industry produces 67 per cent of this total, agriculture 30 per cent and the municipalities about 3 per cent. The average Canadian in an urban area generates 4.3 lbs of solid waste every day, or 1,500 lbs a year.
This represents a tremendous volume of garbage and suitable methods of dealing with it have yet to be developed. I might add that every day increasing numbers of plastic products, which cannot be broken down or recycled, are reaching consumers. This, of course, cannot but add to the difficulty. This is a situation which must be dealt with effectively, but so far I have seen no movement on the part of the government to do so. This is not just a problem which affects one city or a few cities; it is a national problem and is one concerning which the government should be taking action. I submit the government is not doing so.
I wish to conclude with this comment. Disregarding the several gestures which the government has made in response to the demands of the public, it has not yet shown real concern about pollution in Canada and the need for measures of pollution control as a priority: control of pollution is not rated as a first priority, as a second priority or even as a third priority. As I see it, it tags along as an addition to the various areas of responsibility which the government exercises. It is attached to fisheries, it is attached to transport, it is attached to water, it is attached to public health. The intention originally was to centralize responsibility in one department so that effective measures could be taken. I say that though the form was changed and a new department set up, action by that department has been restricted through lack of wholehearted support.
Presumably, the government as a whole believed that the problem would go away or that the people would forget about it. I assure hon. members opposite that neither of these things will happen. The problem will not go away, and as long as people are troubled by evidence of pollution which they can see every day for themselves, they will not forget about it. The challenge to the government is great. I commend the government for the efforts it has made so far in preparing the ground and bringing down legislation. But so far none of this work has been followed up. Regulations putting teeth into these laws have yet to be passed. The large sums of money necessary to make them operative have yet to be provided. The form is there; the shell is there: but to this point it is a hollow shell, devoid of substance.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Weatherhead (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his speech this afternoon the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) outlined just how the tripartite discussions between the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipal governments are once more back on the rails with the meeting in Hull on April 10 next. He also outlined our housing successes of last year consisting of 230,000 housing starts, with great
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems emphasis being placed on public housing, and the hope and expectation is for 240,000 starts this year.
Toward the end of his comments the minister also made reference to our proposed new policies regarding mortgage banks, which are designed to make a mortgage a more liquid security, and to our policy regarding improving drastically the quality of urban neighbourhoods. I thought that tonight I would make a few comments, not so much in my capacity as parliamentary secretary to the minister but more in my original capacity as a member of parliament from the metropolitan Toronto area.
In my first speech in the House of Commons on November 12, 1968, I said I was completely in favour of a new department of urban affairs being established. As reported at page 2652 of Hansard for that date, I said:
-I believe first of all that a new federal department of urban affairs should be created. Such a department would be able to be an effective liaison not only between the various federal departments interested in urban matters but would be able to direct and increase the co-operation among the federal, provincial and municipal levels of government, which is so necessary because of the overlapping constitutional jurisdictions in this field.
Such a new department would also be able to focus federal interest and concern on urban areas and also stimulate research, both in our universities and in the department itself, on urban problems. We have had departments of fisheries and agriculture ever since confederation and now, when most Canadians reside in our cities, I strongly submit that a department of urban affairs, with its own minister in the cabinet, is not only desirable but absolutely necessary.
As I say, I made that speech in this House about 31 years ago and at that time a great many Members of Parliament from different parties, both from Toronto area and elsewhere, were saying somewhat the same thing. I confess that at that time I was not too optimistic about our government's attitude in this respect. It seemed that we had real constitutional problems. As the minister stated this afternoon, it was not a question of using the excuse that the municipalities are under provincial jurisdiction-there is no question of that. It was more a question of how we could become involved more significantly in the field of urban affairs without treading on the toes of the provinces, or at least seeming to do so. However, I must say that with the appointment of the then minister responsible for housing, the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andras), to that portfolio in the spring of 1969, I believe it was, he quietly and effectively came to stress in his speeches, both in the House and outside, the importance of urban matters to the national scene.
The minister also mentioned earlier today that Mr. Harvey Lithwick and other consultants were commissioned to make an in-depth study of the problems facing urban Canada. When that study was published a couple of years ago the statistics and facts contained in the report were enough to convince the government that the time had indeed come to appoint a minister of state for urban affairs. According to the statistics, about 70 per cent of the Canadian people today live in cities. As of 1980, about 80 per cent will live in the cities. Even more significant than that, by the year 2000, if present trends continue, approximately 73 per cent of Canadians will live in our largest 12 urban cities, about 45 per cent of these-almost

March 13, 1972
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems half-living in the cities of Montreal, Vancouver and Toronto.
According to a projection to the year 2000, the city of Toronto will then have six million people, as against only about two million now, a figure which most people regard as too many. Without being facetious, the fact that by the year 2000 Toronto will have six million people living in the city is enough to demonstrate to the federal government the necessity for a ministry of urban affairs. One has now been created.
As illustrated in the speeches of the former minister, as well as the new minister of the department, 27 federal departments and agencies and 112 federal programs directly relate to urban Canada. Therefore, we have to be able to co-ordinate all of these federal departments and agencies and, more importantly, federal programs, and direct their thrust at the urban areas. We must also stimulate liaison between the provinces and municipalities, which is one of the objectives of the new ministry. Then, of course, we must facilitate urban research both at universities and in the urban ministry itself.
It is quite easy to say that we do not need studies of this kind or that kind, but may I remind hop. members that that it was the study conducted by Mr. Lithwick, as well as studies of a similar kind, that graphically showed just where the country was heading as far as urban Canada is concerned and underlined the importance of urban affairs to the national scene. So I suggest that studies of this kind are very important.
As I have said, liaison between the federal government, the provinces and the municipalities is very important, especially when there are municipalities the size of Toronto within which some two million people are living under a system of regional government. There are other municipalities in Canada of similar size, which means that in terms of population they are larger than some of the provinces. It is extremely important to maintain close co-operation with large municipalities of this kind.
If I may say something about the Toronto area and federal concerns in the field of urban affairs, I suppose the classic and most recent case is the proposed new airport to be constructed in the Pickering area. The history of this airport is quite well known but perhaps I could refer to it briefly for a minute or so. The House will recall that in the fall of 1968 the then minister of transport, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer), announced that the federal government intended to expand the area of Malton airport, increase the terminal facilities and also runway facilities so long as any land expansion in the area met with the approval of the people living in surrounding communities. That was the basis on which the minister's plans were presented.
Led by members of parliament from the area west of metropolitan Toronto, such as the hon. member for Lake-shore (Mr. Robinson), the hon. member for Etobicoke (Mr. Gillespie), who is presently Minister of State for Science and Technology, the then hon. member for York West (Mr. Givens) and the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Chappell), the federal government was persuaded that an expansion of this area would be too detrimental to the people living in the surrounding district. This area was entirely built up to the west and south, and also somewhat

to the north and east. After a great many consultations with the municipalities in the area, the federal government kept its promise and while it decided to considerably increase terminal and runway facilities at Malton it did not expropriate or acquire any more land in the Malton area.
During the last three years, about $80 million of federal money has gone into the Malton airport and into improving transportation facilities there. A new terminal is to be opened on July 1, I believe, of this year with much additional runway space to be completed at the same time. However, there is still great need for a second airport in the Toronto and southern Ontario region.
The federal government made an extensive search of potential sites in the southern Ontario region from Lake Simcoe past Hamilton toward Lake Scugoc in the east. With the co-operation of the federal government and the general desire of the provincial government, the site was finally located, as announced a week or so ago, in the Pickering area. Why was it located there? This is a project involving $350 million or so and, in addition, at least as much provincial money will probably be involved, before the project is over, through acquiring the surrounding land for commerial and housing purposes. It was placed to the east of Toronto in order to coincide completely with the provincial government. The Toronto centred regional plan-the blue book which the provincial government brought out in May, 1970-stressed that the area to the west of Toronto was being built up quickly and there was no need for further stimulus in that area. Instead, the provincial government would like to develop the area east of Toronto which had been going forward fairly slowly, comparatively speaking. I may say that the new ministry of state for urban affairs had considerable input, as it should have, in this particular decision.
The members of that ministry and the ministers themselves-the former and present ministers-were very strong in agreeing with the general concept for the plan for urban development in the Toronto area. They wanted to co-operate with the province in this regard because they thought it was by and large a good concept. Therefore, after considerable negotiation and some delay caused by the provincial leadership campaign and the provincial general election, we heard in the past couple of weeks the announcement of the location of the second Toronto airport. This was a joint announcement of the provincial and federal governments. They agreed 100 per cent with this particular location. I do not think there is any question that the second airport is needed, because the Toronto-southern Ontario area is the most populous area in the country. We are the business centre of the country. Also, because of the multicultural nature of so many of our people there is considerable air traffic between the Toronto area and countries in Europe.
I do not believe there is any doubt that the people in the region as a whole will be happy to see the airport develop. However, at this time I believe we must exercise great care in respect of the people in Pickering and the surrounding area who will be affected by the airport. Under the Expropriation Act passed a few years ago in this House, the people in this area, and indeed many others in
March 13, 1972

the country who have objection to a second airport, will be given the right to attend hearings particularly set up for this purpose, at which they will be able to argue as strongly as they wish that the airport should not be located in the Pickering area but somewhere else.
However, if the courts should rule that the governments concerned may expropriate the area in question, I believe it will be up to the people themselves, including their representatives and local members of parliament from the area, to make sure they receive the highest compensation the law will allow, not only for the land itself but for disturbance and moving expenses as well as anything else for which an allowance might be made.
There is no doubt that the airport in this region will create a hardship for many people in the Pickering area. If an airport in any part of southern Ontario is to be of any use to the people as a whole, it will be a hardship to the people located in that area. I believe the people will have every opportunity to present their full case to the boards or courts in question and will be treated very fairly so far as compensation is concerned.
What are some other federal projects of interest in the Toronto area which come under the general urban affairs connotation? We have the problem of commuter rail transportation to the Toronto area. As we know, in many cities in North America, and in many cities in Europe, commuter rail transportation to and from our large cities is quite a common occurrence. This, however, has not been the case in the Toronto area. Our people have been accustomed to coming into the city by and large by automobile; they have not used trains because train service has not been available. Under the aegis of the chairman of metropolitan Toronto, Mr. Campbell, a joint commuter rail study was set up in the spring of last year between metropolitan Toronto, the railways and the provincial government. This study involved, in considerable detail, an examination into the various options so far as rail service to the Toronto area is concerned. I understand this study is to be completed by May of this year and I trust the report will be made available at that time.
We, of course, have the same difficulties as other major cities. As the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) indicated, there is the difficulty of cars coming in great numbers into the downtown area and choking it. We may be able to use our excellent railway lines coming into the city in order to take some of the pressure off the highways.
We also have the question of the somewhat controversial metro centre project in Toronto. The federal government would be involved in the metro centre concept because the two Crown corporations would be quite heavily involved in the project if it proceeds. The CNR is a partner in the project with the CPR, and the CBC has a considerable interest in it. The CBC would like to locate its main transmission centre in that location and consolidate its other services in the Toronto area in this central location. The CNR and CBC, I understand, would look to the federal government for financial assistance to help them locate in the new metro centre area. As hon. members are aware, the city government has approved the plans and the provincial government has referred the
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems metro centre plan to the Ontario Municipal Board for final determination.
The metro centre concept has come under attack from national groups, including the amalgamated group known as CORRA which is protesting some aspects of the plan. I think it is excellent that the ratepayers' group in particular is taking a direct interest in this plan which would change completely the downtown area, with heavy federal financial assistance. This should be considered carefully. It is interesting to note that on one hand the federal government will be heavily involved in the plan and on the other the federal government has in the past, through CMHC and other federal departments, financed CORRA is some of its activities. So we are seeing direct citizens' participation in this project. If the municipal board decides that the plan can go ahead, perhaps with some amendments, we will see great changes in the downtown area of the city.
I might mention the possibility of a dome stadium in the Toronto area and of the federal government being involved in such a project. Again, this is a controversial matter, a matter of federally-owned land in the Downs-view airport area which might be made available by sale or, more probably, by lease to an organization or to a non-profit group for sports purposes. I could mention a number of other projects, but my time is rapidly terminating.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF THE GOVERNMENT TO CO-OPERATE WITH PROVINCIAL AND MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS IN DEALING WITH URBAN PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), made under mysterious circumstances on the weekend, have any truth to them, he would be the only prime minister in history who would go into an election campaign with a rather interesting statistic to lay before the people-that is, if this parliament lasts until next year into the fall and the government has gone its full five years plus. He would be able to say that over one million housing units have been built in his term of office, an impressive statistic but also one that has paradoxical disadvantages for the government because that sort of statistic would quite easily prove that the right hon. gentleman has not succeeded in establishing the merits of his so-called just society.
I shall proceed to explain the paradox in a moment, but first let me warm up with the reflection that housing has many economic ramifications. It is one of the largest single industries in the country; it is an enormous consumer of capital and resources and it is the livelihood of many professions and trades. It is also very much a social enterprise in that it supplies a commodity without which men cannot live in this climate. We all know what the great Canadian winter is all about, something to be endured and generally not enjoyed, and without which families cannot enjoy feelings or well being, security, dignity and social justice.
Housing is a necessity. Yet too often federal policies submerge this necessity or make it play a secondary role

March 13, 1972
Fedpral Co-operation in Urban Problems to temporary financial and credit measures. In his interesting speech to the Canadian Conference on Housing in 1968, the English expert in this field, David V. Donnison pointed out:
-housing is too big a sphere of responsibility to be cornered by one department, and it could not be dealt with effectively if it was. Housing policies are a matter for governments as a whole, and many departments and levels of government-federal, provincial and local-must play a part in formulating and implementing them. The task is a complex and continually changing one which each country must pursue in ways that suit its own needs and resources.
We all recall the tremendous efforts that have been made in this Parliament over the years to get government to take even the timid step of appointing somebody as minister of one of these new state creations, let alone putting him in charge of a fully-fledged department of urban affairs as would be done very quickly under a change in the prime ministership of this country.
The former and first holder of that ministry has said that the government has been the driving force behind 750,000 new housing starts, yet a CMHC survey in 1970 revealed that less than 16 per cent of all new houses for sale in that year were priced at under $20,000, and the average that year was $28,614. Fewer than 7 per cent of Canadians can afford homes with that kind of a price tag upon them. That is where, as I said at the outset of my remarks, is the paradox of the just society which enters into the housing picture.
Let us examine further illustrations in this field. Let us take the statistics of CMHC and borrowings under the National Housing Act. In 1968, the lower income third of the population of this country took 6.5 per cent of the money available for housing, the middle income third took 49.4 per cent and the upper income third took 44.1 per cent. Two years later the figures in those three respective categories were 5.3 per cent, 54.2 per cent and 40.5 per cent.
If you want to show how rapidly the position of lower income Canadians has deteriorated in almost the last decade, note that in 1965 the lower income third share of the borrowings was 17.9 per cent, which shrunk to 5.3 per cent in 1970-an almost incredible statistic and an almost incredible indictment of the government in the housing policy that simply does not permit the little Canadian to have his share in home ownership. I think this is the most serious problem that could possibly be faced in the overall housing field.
Therefore I say that there must be a greater federal role in enabling home ownership for the lower income groups of Canadians. There are some provinces, namely Ontario, Nova Scotia and others, that are waging this battle to give the lower income Canadian his place in the housing sun. On several occasions I made the suggestion to the former minister that more had to be done by him and by his government. I give him fair notice that this plea will be followed up when he takes his statistics into one of the House committees for study. That is one area where a change must be made; but it is the most obvious one where a change of heart, a change of direction and a change of the money flow is needed.
Let us examine briefly some of the other points with which a Conservative administration would concern itself

in this very important field. One is the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials, one of the most iniquitous levies ever put on a social necessity. Also, we must realize that there are one million substandard homes in Canada, 250,000 of them in a state of serious disrepair. Leaving the centre of cities rotting until it is too late to do much about them, and then entering into costly clearing schemes, has simply proved to be an insufficient answer. A better cure, and one that is available, is a revamping of the home improvement loans plan.
The fourth thing that should be done is to provide greater tax incentives for the developers. The fifth thing that should be done is to make CMHC regulations easier for the man or woman who wants to live in rural Canada, to make it easier for that person to obtain mortgage financing. In my province there is only one company, privately owned, that does a real job in that field and one other company that does part of a job. Guess where the great, Crown lending agency fits in, Mr. Speaker? It fits in with the also-rans that really do no job at all. CMHC and housing policy must recognize the realities of rural living and needs.
Sixth, if one gets to the problem of growth in the cities and we accept the idea of designated growth areas, as some government departments have done, then surely CMHC and housing policies must recognize such growth concepts. That is why I mentioned earlier the absolute need for a housing policy that not only reflects an increased stature for this strange ministry that has been created in recent months but that will put some hair on its chest, if I may use that expression when speaking to the minister.

subsubtopic: COMMONS REBATES
speechtext: That isn't fair.

subsubtopic: COMMONS REBATES
speechtext: The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) has come alive.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: COMMONS REBATES
speechtext: Some people wish they had hair in other places.

subsubtopic: COMMONS REBATES
speechtext:
As my seventh point, I suggest putting hair on the chest of the department. The eighth thing that needs to be done is to establish a national urban council to work on and advise the government on a national urban policy. Perhaps the closest we have to that is the Community Planning Association of Canada. Last year it conducted a survey of people interested in urban affairs problems and came up with a six-point synopsis of the major issues. I wish to put them on the record, quoting from a brief that was submitted to the former minister of state for urban affairs:
1.	That Canadians have a major concern for the future of their cities.
2.	That Canadians are anxious to express their aspirations for the city but do not know how to do so.
This is a brief for Information Canada. This is a real challenge for them.
3.	That Canadians are entirely convinced that government must listen to the citizen's viewpoint on urban affairs and that it must be able to utilize such a citizen input.
March 13, 1972

4.	That, although Canadians are aware of the various levels of government, it is the local level (because of its immediacy) to which they relate.
5.	That most Canadians demand a strengthening of local government.
6.	That Canadians, as citizens, are insistent upon their involvement in the development of a Canadian urban policy and that government provide for them to be so involved.
With the kind of attitude shown in that survey it is quite obvious that the government, and particularly this minister, are considered to be a long way from meeting the needs of our times. Further, Sir, to strengthen the need for the development of an urban national council to give advice may I make this argument briefly, one which I have made time and time again, namely, that it will be difficult for any government to solve the problem that is bursting upon us with almost frightening rapidity, that is, the growth of the megalopolis stretching from Montreal along the St. Lawrence Seaway to Detroit, Chicago and Milwaukee which by the turn of the century, and probably before then, will have a greater concentration of people than the Atlantic seabord megalopolis stretching between Boston and Baltimore. Those of us who have travelled through the latter area know that it is really one large city: you cannot tell one place from another except by the landmarks. It is an antheap of humanity crying out with problems concerning transportation, crime, housing, health-every type of problem under the sun-aggravated because people are living together in almost inhuman conditions.
That is exactly what is developing in Canada. And there is a lesson to be learned. How effective has the American federal government been in co-operating with the states and the huge cities that make up its megalopolis terrain area? At least we have an example to learn from, an example of what is happening. I suggest that the problems there have not really been successfully handled. From this example we can see the handwriting on the wall for the present government and the government that will succeed it. The federal government must do something, and do it quickly, to involve all levels of government in tackling this problem. This involvement perhaps may be harshly different from anything that has been attempted up until now. It is a problem that has to be solved, otherwise the Canadian way of life that we talk about so much will be no better than the American way of life, and perhaps we will be worse off simply because we have not been bright enough to learn from the experience that the Americans are undergoing.
The Americans have hang-ups about transportation in their crowded corridor. In this context it was interesting to hear the remarks made by speakers in this debate on transportation matters. For instance, the preceding speaker and others put in a thoughtful plug on a very serious matter indeed. All these things, transportation, housing needs, planning needs, health needs, the use of water resources and the fight against pollution-all those creations of a Frankenstein that should frighten hell out of any government-point out the necessity for a lot more zip, a lot more consideration by the government and by this particular minister with respect to something we are rapidly facing, a change in our Canadian way of life.

Mr. Speaker, many hon. members from the other side used quotations from newspapers in their speeches and I want to follow their example.

2	the brief reads:
-we must now set goals for a balanced socio-economic program, giving due importance to the quality of shelter, to open space and recreation, to health services, to conservation measures for water, air and other natural resources, to balanced systems of transportation for people and goods in and around urban areas and, not least in difficulty and expense, to the disposal and recycling of wastes.
They go on to give many details. Some hon. members who have spoken mentioned underground wiring, other

March 13, 1972
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems underground services and such things which are a requirement in any new development. In fact, they are necessary and should be provided as we go along so that we do not fact the same problems as were faced 30 or 40 years ago. But, Mr. Speaker, it does not matter how it is done, it is always the same taxpayer who pays the bill- the fellow who purchases the house or rents it. He has to pay for all the services, the schools and parks, whatever is provided. I agree with many things that have been said, and possibly lower rates of interest should be considered. One thing that should be considered once and for all is the elimination of school taxes, at least in my province. This would be a great change and would certainly help newcomers who are just going into housing and senior citizens who are moving into senior citizens' homes. The latter should not be paying the heavy cost of development and should get some relief from taxes.
Referring to an intergovernmental council on community development, the brief continues:
Under conditions of increasing insecurity for the citizen, and in the face of threats of environmental deterioration, it is the local officials who feel the first impact of public concern. Mayors and councillors, being of the level of government closest to the people, are very often blamed and held responsible for programs and policies, or lack of them that originate at the federal and/or provincial levels. Many Canadian citizens claim they are the victims of economic dislocation, technological change and the kind of misallocation of resources that gravely threaten their standards of living. Local government has no choice but to demand a co-ordination of the efforts of all levels of government toward the attainment of economic growth and improvement in human well-being.
This is what the federation had to say last year. They also made some recommendations which I think are important, as set out at pages 4 and 5 of the brief as follows:
1.	"areas requiring special measures" be redefined to rid us of the anomaly of the ineligibility of urban slums for federal-provincial financial assistance by virtue of their proximity to affluent suburbs. The deprived in Victoria suffer as much hardship as those in Halifax.

3.	the federal government pursue its objectives of creating a ministry of state responsible for urban affairs-
The brief continues:
We are also concerned with the apparent intent to exclude nonurban communities from the anticipated trilevel consultations.
The concluding paragraph in that section reads:
For these reasons we endorse the proposal for a trilevel forum- an intergovernmental council on community development-to provide for the free exchange of views by federal, provincial and local policy makers; a forum that would enable all governments to clarify their roles in providing leadership, direction and action in response to the real need of our citizens.
I think this spells out what local governments all across the country are concerned with, and I think they know the problems better than anybody else. They have often made good representations which possibly have been overlooked at times. When they make their recommendations at the end of this month, I hope due consideration will be given to them.

The federal government is willing to reduce its powers in the field of urban development, if that reduction leads to federal-provincial co-operation-

-in the redevelopment of Canadian cities, urban affairs minister Robert Andras said in Montreal yesterday. And in this sense, by putting its urban policies and programs on the table for discussion, the federal government is, if anything, permitting a lessening of its powers rather than the reverse: seeking to intrude into an area of provincial jurisdiction."
He went on to make several comments along the lines on which I have been speaking tonight. I hope that the Federation of Mayors and Municipalities will continue to apply pressure when they present their briefs because I think we could benefit from many of their recommendations.
When the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Weatherhead) spoke a short while ago he said, among other things, that consideration should be given to building a dome stadium in his area. I did not think I would be standing up tonight and saying that since the government is to build a second, multimillion dollar airport in the Toronto area, why does it not build a domed stadium for mine. Surely to goodness western Canada needs one or two facilities like that, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: COMMONS REBATES
speechtext: I should like nothing better than to see a domed stadium built in Winnipeg so that we could see all sorts of finals and football games in our area without being snowed out or rained under.

subsubtopic: COMMONS REBATES
speechtext:
An hon. member mentioned Vancouver. I thought we might begin where the west begins and go on from there. They did that with the railroad, by the way. Seriously, Mr. Speaker, I think a domed stadium should be considered for that area. Many other facilities might be considered. The point is that as was spelled out this afternoon the area municipality, in co-operation with other levels of governments, might solve some of the problems affecting the area. No matter whether proposed projects involve slum clearance, urban renewal, new development-call them what you will-all the citizens of the area and of the country will benefit if money is spent in that way. I think there is no better way of spending money than on programs which municipal governments at present most earnestly need. Those programs can be carried out in co-operation with provincial governments. If the minister-who is here-takes my representations into consideration as well as the represen-
March 13, 1972

tations which will be made to him shortly, he will go a long way toward meeting the demands of certain municipalities and we shall solve many of our problems to the ultimate benefit of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: COMMONS REBATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I heard that the minister to whom we listened this afternoon had assumed the portfolio of urban affairs, I felt a degree of sympathy for him because of the awesome task that he had taken upon himself. The problems of the cities are formidable and growing ever more formidable as time goes on. Problems of unemployment, poverty, housing, pollution, financing, as well as many more, call for Herculean efforts of leadership if there are to be solutions.
As I listened this afternoon to the smooth-flowing discourse of the minister, I realized once again that what this government says and what it does are worlds apart. Indeed, the minister's speech made me realize that the policies of this government are made by comfortable people for comfortable people who delude themselves into thinking that while there may be a few unemployed, sick or handicapped people around, with a little more effort on their part they could join the ranks of the affluent instead of allowing themselves to depend on the taxpayer for social assistance.
The minister waxed lyrical over our urban possibilities and over the opportunity to "create a society of exceptional excellence" in Canada, yet he overlooked the need to take the first urgent steps to that end. One of the most urgent of those is the matter of housing for low-income people in the big cities, although rural areas have also been shamefully neglected. He boasted of what he calls the government's colossal housing program and of the number of housing starts in 1971. I ask, housing starts for whom?
Less than 10 per cent of housing starts in 1971 were for subsidized public housing. That is the only kind of housing the poor can afford. Long lines of them wait patiently for clean, warm shelter while the National Housing Act serves those who are in less need of help. The National Housing Act was supposed to help people on low income. What are the facts, Mr. Speaker? As the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) said, in 1970 the lowest income third of families borrowing under the National Housing Act amounted to only 5.3 per cent of the total. These were people with incomes of up to $7,000. So we have a National Housing Act that under this government's policy provides almost 95 per cent of its resources for the service of people with incomes of $7,000 and over. The other 5 per cent of resources go to those with incomes of under $7,000. Clearly, the poor get only the crumbs.
The minister may say all he likes about research into housing, new products and new ways of doing things. The fact remains that those on low income are getting the short end of the stick and are very likely to continue doing so. And it is a very short end indeed. The only satisfactory way to provide for the needs of the poor is to provide them with income.
Mr. Speaker, income and options go together. When those who are poor can get income and the means of earning it, they can and will decide on the kind of place in
Federal Co-operation in Urban Problems
which they want to live; and it will not be a high-rise, urban ghetto. There are already far too many of these areas in Canada.
In January of this year a four year-old boy was fatally injured when he fell from a seventh-floor balcony in Toronto. He was still conscious when his mother picked him up. He was crying, "Mummy, Mummy." He died three hours later. That was the seventh time this year a child has fallen from an upper storey window or balcony in metropolitan Toronto. Studies have shown that housewives and children living on the upper floors of high-rise buildings are far more prone to illness, physical and nervous, than those living near the ground.
Meanwhile, until poor people cannot obtain the kind of income that will enable them to get the kind of housing they want, let me urge upon the minister that every sort of public housing ought to provide adequate play-spaces and facilities, both indoor and outside, and that there should be child-care facilities either in the project or in a community centre nearby. The minister knows Vancouver very well. He knows the need is there and he knows it is not being met. I urge him to use the National Housing Act and make the provision of such facilities mandatory.

I suggest that the minister explore the possibility of introducing a number of low-income families into co-operative housing developments, such as is being done now in the De Cosmos village co-operative project in the Vancouver area. Actually, they were overjoyed at being able to get away from the stigma that is attached to the residents of ordinary low-rent projects.
Every report we get from every committee and authority concerned with urban problems stresses the need of adequate income for those who are poor. Enough income means a chance to live in modern, well planned neighbourhoods, a chance to get away from the heavily congested core areas and a chance to give their children an opportunity to associate with other children free from the stigma of poverty and insecurity. And, Mr. Speaker, that is a very real stigma in the minds of people receiving social assistance or on low income.

subsubtopic: COMMONS REBATES
speechtext: Especially in the minds of the young.

subsubtopic: COMMONS REBATES
speechtext:
We are beginning to realize the social costs of keeping poverty. The Lithwick study refers to the way in which women heads of families are rendered particularly immobile because we have no day-care system to help them. The elderly, the handicapped, the unemployed and chronically ill are chained remorselessly to their situation by lack of income. They are chained with all the cruelty of chains in a medieval dungeon. Their options are non-existent and their numbers are growing. If the minister will not use the National Housing Act to provide daycare facilities in each project or, where that is not desirable, in community centres nearby, he should do something which would cause his name to be inscribed on bronze plates around Vancouver. I would take pleasure in seeing that he got one or two.
What about the dollars and cents cost of keeping poverty? The welfare system at all levels costs the Canadian taxpayer more than $6 billion a year. The Senate Committee on Poverty said:
The welfare system, at all levels, costs Canadians more than six billion a year, yet it has not significantly alleviated poverty let alone eliminated it. The problems grow; costs go up and up and will, in time, suffocate the taxpayer. The welfare system is increasingly unable to deal with the needs of its clients. It has failed to acheive its humanitarian goals. It deprives its recipients of dignity and provides no incentive or rewards to escape from poverty. It has become punitive and demeaning. It is a mess-a social wasteland and an economic morass.
So much for the Senate Committee on Poverty. Poverty is a waste, an intolerable frustration and a soul-destroying torture to those caught in the morass. We can no longer afford it. The only way to wipe it out is to provide income for the poor. All the housing reports say so, a decent income based on the cost of living index and rising with it. Along with this must go opportunities for useful activity in the community according to the measure of one's ability to serve.
My earnest suggestion to the minister is that he approach his colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and any other colleagues necessary with a view to finding ways and means of building an income floor beneath which no Canadian will be allowed to fall. In my view, this would be a major step in dealing with one of the most serious urban problems, the problem of poverty and insufficient income. It would lighten enormously the burden of the minister in dealing with other urban problems if he could make a frontal attack on this core problem of poverty. It is not going to stay in the core; it will spread in ever-widening circles to get people enslaved.
There is also the problem of urban traffic. I feel sure that in his heart the minister knows we should now consider the moving of people rather than providing endless transport facilities for cars. I feel certain he realizes that to divide and destroy neighbourhoods by great, noisy freeways is to move away from the dreams of a society of exceptional excellence. The remarks of the minister at various times in Vancouver have shown that he is aware of a rising feeling in the community, that what is immediately required is not a third crossing of Burrard Inlet which would benefit only a limited number of citizens, but

a well planned system of rapid transit which would serve the whole metropolitan area. Why then does he not involve himself as Minister of Urban Affairs? He must involve himself because some of his colleagues are taking the opposite side of the coin and saying that we must have a third crossing of Burrard Inlet. They say this must be the first priority. The minister owes it to the people of this country to take the initiative and say where he stands.
The minister has talked of the need for rapid transit. He has indicated that even though a certain portion of the population wants a third crossing, Ottawa should not be content to give a grant for it but should use it for rapid transit if the majority wants that. Why, then, as Minister of Urban Affairs can he not become involved and take the initiative in getting that rapid transit system instead of the third crossing?
The minister has talked of the need for tripartite consultation and planning in these matters. Let him now take the initiative and convene a meeting of the other levels of government to discuss the best course to follow from the standpoint of the whole community rather than that of special groups and interests. I am sure that such action on his part would be infinitely more impressive than hours of talk about the need for co-operation.
If the minister announced that he was seeking the cooperation of provincial and municipal authorities for this purpose, I am sure that neither of those levels of government would dare refuse him a meeting. If he does not do that, he is open to a charge of fence-sitting and staying clear because he wants to stand well with certain groups and interests. He can smile pleasantly and look like the smiling Buddha all he likes, but the people are likely to discover that smiling Buddha is not what they need right now. They want a man of action, a man who will act in the interest of the whole community of Vancouver, someone who is not afraid even if he is called a hamburger by the head of the city or runs the risk of being called a bigot by the premier of that province. I do not know the danger in that regard.
In my view, in addition to tripartite consultation there should be a fourth level, those interested community groups which are becoming the counterweight to the pressures of special privilege which exist on every hand. We discovered the value of such volunteer community groups during the debate of the Canada Water Act when the efforts of anti-pollution groups all across Canada succeeded in stopping the great detergent companies from continuing to ruin the waterways with high concentrations of phosphates. In that instance, the then Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was exceedingly glad of the pressure of those volunteer groups which helped to get the anti-phosphate provision into the Canada Water Act.
This minister can, if he will, discover the value of such voluntary groups in the stiff battles that lie ahead to preserve and improve the quality of urban environment. He should welcome the pressures which have fought for things like keeping the quality of the environment in the entrance to Stanley Park and preventing such horrors as the Four Seasons which would block the entrance to Stanley Park, cut off the view and make the traffic far more contested at that point that it would otherwise be.

I fixed all that up last week.
March 13, 1972

subsubtopic: COMMONS REBATES
speechtext:
The minister may have fixed all that up, but will it stay fixed? Mr. Fix-It may have fixed it for a while, but he is no white knight on a white charger coming to clean up things in the way the advertisers claim. Ajax will not work without public opinion and public organization behind him.
As I say, this minister can, if he will, discover their value in the stiff battles ahead to preserve and improve the quality of urban environment. Problems like air pollution, industrial and domestic waste, the proper use of land, the saving of recreational areas and many others can be solved satisfactorily only with the co-operation of all levels of government plus the growing strength of well organized and well informed community groups. The minister is well aware of this. He also knows how to take advantage of those groups when there is pressure, if he wants to do the job. I hope he wants to do it.
Looking at the unplanned chaos of our great cities, we are becoming aware that unless something far-reaching is done soon the whole population is headed for serious trouble. It is in the cities that we see the full impact of poverty and pollution, the effects of bad housing and an unwholesome environment on whole areas of chronically unemployed people, their families, the unskilled, poorly educated, crippled, aged, one-parent families the idle young people, thousands of individuals doomed to struggle uselessly in the trap of poverty, condemned to raise their children there and in turn watch them struggle vainly to escape, only to subside into frustration and bitterness or to gamble desperately with law breaking and revolt. One can look at the great cities south of the border to see what happens when cities get bigger-the numbers of poor people increase and nothing adequate is done about it.
If the home is to be the cradle of citizenship, let the Minister of Urban Affairs take as his first priority the giving of leadership in the building of homes and neighbourhoods fit for the future citizens of this country, beginning with those whose need is the greatest, the people with low incomes. Let him not rest content until every Canadian has enough income to lift himself or herself out of poverty and enough opportunity to contribute something of value to the Canadian community. Let him not take refuge in quoting statistics which tell only part of the story. Let him get busy and make statistics of his own, figures which can stand the light of day and which can be divulged without fear of the consequences to the government.

subsubtopic: HIGHWAYS-TWINNING OF TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY- ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST YELLOWHEAD PASS ROUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 8, as reported at page 638 of Hansard, I directed the following question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube):
Would the minister please advise the House why his department made the decision to twin the southern part of the Trans-Canada Highway in Alberta leading to Banff and discriminate against the Yellowhead Trans-Canada Highway which is the northern counterpart.
Although briefs have been presented by the interdepartmental highway and road co-ordinating committee to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) and to the former minister of public works, I find the government playing politics and spending money twinning the Banff-Jasper highway while forgetting to upgrade the Yellowhead highway to trans-Canada standards so that other communities might enjoy a new recreational, commercial and industrial communications corridor. This highway will have a great bearing on the future development of Canada as a viable and expanding nation. It will play a vital role in the development of the vast areas of natural resources it serves, and the efforts which have been expended on the roads to resources program by all levels of government will bear this out.
The minister should be made aware of the tremendous difficulties being presented at this time in connection with the route which was accepted as the trans-Canada route, particularly through the Rocky Mountains section of that highway in Alberta and British Columbia where, due to heavy snowfalls, the danger of avalanches is always prevalent during the winter months. This, combined with high railway transportation costs which result from these unfavourable conditions, presents an economic picture

March 13, 1972
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion which must affect not only the transport facilities available to Canadians but the development of our export trade.
The key to the Yellowhead route is that it takes advantage of the finest pass in the Canadian Rockies at an elevation of some 2,000 feet less than that of Rogers Pass. At its highest snowfall level, this route experiences less than 50 per cent of the snow recorded on the other route over a long period. Climatic conditions along the two routes vary widely. The most undesirable of climatic conditions affecting motor travel is doubtless snowfall and its accompanying hazards. Along one path of the Yellowhead the most severe snowfall occurs at Blue River, approximately 146 miles northeast by road from Kamloops where an average 159 inches falls annually over the long term. Secondary to this, the average annual snowfall at Red Pass, some 42 miles west of Jasper, is 137 inches. These two spots represent the only two major areas where snowfall is significantly greater than would be encountered across the Prairies. At no point along the entire route is snowfall heavy enough to present the danger of an avalanche. Thus, the danger of snowslides does not exist along the Yellowhead.
This is not the case, however, along the Rogers Pass section of the trans-Canada highway. Rogers Pass experiences one of the highest recorded annual snowfalls in Canada. The long-term average is 370 inches per year. Further, even at Lake Louise, only 50 miles or so into the Rockies, snowfall approaches 200 inches per year, greater than at any point along the Yellowhead route. Road closures due to avalanches or to the danger of avalanches are a frequent occurrence along the southern route, seriously hampering the scheduling of passage of vehicles using it during the winter. An analysis of the statistics makes it obvious that on a year-round basis, due to elevation and grades, and on a seasonal basis due to snowfall, the Yellowhead route is not just an alternative route between the Prairies and the coast: it is, indeed, a much superior one.

subsubtopic: DRUGS-REQUEST THAT FURTHER REPORTS OF LE DAIN COMMISSION BE WITHHELD PENDING INCLUSION OF CAUTIONARY FOREWORD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Le Dain interim report of May, 1970, and the latest part of the report entitled "Treatment" have many well documented errors and inadequacies. These are the product of bias and incomplete research. I suggest to this House that we must insist that the expected publication and distribution of the Le Dain commission's forthcoming major study on cannabis be withheld from public distribution until a team of leading Canadian medical scientists has examined it carefully.
Ten prominent Canadian doctors proposed this measure in a Canadian Press statement of October 14, 1971, to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and to the federal and provincial ministers of health and welfare, and justice. "Silence must end," they said, denouncing the interim report of the Le Dain commission. "In our judgment, the Le Dain commission showed both bias and social and scientific irresponsibility" in some of the evidence presented, while "evidence of the harmful effects of this drug, cannabis, was buried under hundreds of pages so that no clear warning could be derived by an uncritical reader". The signers included the former head of the Canadian Psychiatric Association and doctors associated with six prominent Canadian universities and hospitals.
I also have a 70-page study of the interim report prepared by Dr. Fred Lundell, eminent practitioner, associate professor of psychiatry at McGill University and head of a hospital drug research team, which criticizes the interim report in these words: "The studies selected for discussion were highly edited and hardly current" and, further, "Serious reactions-to cannabis-do occur with greater frequency and more severe consequences than suggested in the report".
Dr. Conrad Swartz, prominent drug research specialist and chief psychiatrist at the student health centre, University of British Columbia, in his study of the interim report
March 13, 1972

cites an example where the report "omits some of the prime statements of the 1968 British commission study entitled 'Cannabis' which would discourage any suggestions that cannabis be legalized".
Dr. Andrew Malcolm, a well known practising psychiatrist of Toronto, who has devoted the past ten years to a study of the illegal use of drugs as a senior officer with the Ontario Addiction Research Foundation, gave to the Canadian Press and the Canadian Medical Association on January 31, 1972, a detailed analysis of the first volume of the Le Dain commission's final report entitled "Treatment", followed by a highly detailed medical criticism of chapter VI of the treatment report on February 20, 1972. Admitting that the treatment report contains much information that is perfectly acceptable, it is, he states, "frequently out of date; it contains a staggering amount of misinformation; its proposals are often misquoted and unrealistic". Dr. Malcolm then detailed 22 major and minor errors.
Equally serious is the February 14 Canadian Medical Association's press statement about the treatment report. After mild praise and acceptance of some recommendations, the CMA statement makes the startling request "that the federal government consider attaching a letter to the report to bring it up to date and to make the important corrections that are required" before sending it out to Canadian doctors and medical institutions.
Imagine the implications when medical experts say we should correct the Le Dain report before sending it out for doctors to use as a "manual of treatment" on Canadian citizens! I am informed that proper information was available to Le Dain in ample time to have been included in the manual. This is inexcusable. The British Columbia Medical Association in a statement to the press on March 10 said;
In our opinion the section on short-term medical management contains so many confusion and questionable points that its distribution to physicians, hospitals and agencies in its present form would only tend to destroy the credibility of the commission in the eyes of many professionals. We request that this chapter VI of the report be not sent to physicians in British Columbia until either it is rewritten or accompanied by a detailed list of corrections of the points which we and others have noted.
It further added:
We are concerned at the rather casual approach in this document to LSD and cannabis.
I am informed that certain other provincial medical associations are equally critical and will soon make their reports public. These documents, and the one to come, cost the Canadian taxpayer $3 million. The British Columbia Medical Association also strongly criticized Le Dain for not making use of the important work of Dr. Andrew Malcolm. I am disturbed that immediately following his public criticism of the Le Dain treatment volume, Dr. Malcolm was fired on one day's notice by the Ontario Addiction Research Foundation, after ten years' service, on the grounds of budget requirements. The March 10 edition of the Toronto Sun states the firing "was the latest in what critics claim is a dispute over the foundation's alleged tacit support of legalizing marijuana."
In view of the Commission's bad track record in its first two publications, I fully support the insistence of the ten eminent Canadian doctors when they say:
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
Our most immediate and grave concern is the possibility that the Le Dain commission may publish a highly permissive fact-hiding and vacillating final report similar to its interim statement of a year ago. Like other commission reports it would be freely available throughout the country and as with the interim report, readership would be promoted and encouraged in some cases by government departments.
And further:
Should the document fail to identify clearly the harmful effects of cannabis use, immense pressures would be created, especially on youth, to increase use of the drug.
It goes on:
If it is placed before the public it must contain a clear and unequivocal statement by the Minister of National Health and Welfare pointing out the extremely serious problem which arises from the taking of soft drugs and the necessity of abstinence at this stage of our knowledge and experience.
For example, the month-old study of the National Institute of Mental Health, reported in the February 28, 1972, edition of U.S. News and World Report, warns, as do the ten doctors, that women of child bearing years would be unwise to use cannabis due to abnormalities found in a few children born of marijuana-smoking mothers, possibly due to the drug and also from experiments with rats which demonstrated serious deformation of offspring as reported in the statement of the ten doctors.
I have also been informed that the so-called leak of the United States President's Commission on Cannabis which appeared in the February 28, 1972, edition of Time magazine does not properly represent the findings of the commission, which are to be published in Washington in late March. To further support their concern, the ten Canadian doctors strongly condemn the recent commission on youth report prepared for the Secretary of State for its "inexcusably dangerous claim" that, in the words of the youth commission, "soft drugs are relatively harmless or at least so they seem in the absence of any medical evidence to the contrary". The doctors point out that large amounts of available research suggesting harmful effects are available.
What happened to this youth report? Thousands of copies were distributed across Canada by the Secretary of State's department, including Information Canada. I have a newspaper published by the Canada YMCA last fall called, "It's your turn". It was distributed to all its branches across Canada calling on youth to buy and study this youth report, with special emphasis on its inexcusable drug recommendation and calling on youth to write to the Secretary of State encouraging him to pass laws supporting youth demands.
I therefore implore the government to withhold the public presentation of the cannabis report of the Le Dain commission until a team of appropriate medical experts has examined it. On the team must be Dr. William Craig, head of research for the Department of Health, as well as Drs. Swartz, Malcolm and Lundell. If their findings warrant it, an appropriate, cautionary foreword should then be written warning all readers of the biases, inaccuracies and incomplete information and advising them of the danger of soft drug use in the light of our present incomplete knowledge. Such action would be one of responsibility toward one of the most vital social problems of the day. If soft drugs are not harmful, we should not restrict

March 13, 1972
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion their sale. If they are harmful, the law should contain certain restrictions.

On such an important matter involving the health of so many Canadians, the minister and his department would be expected to consult, if necessary, members of the medical profession and would also rely on the collaboration of those national bodies specializing in the health care of Canadians.
